controls_moving_around.title: Controls: Moving Around
controls_moving_around.description: You walk with the arrow keys or WASD. Z (or Enter) is confirm and talk, X (or Escape) is cancel and it also opens the pause menu. Holding Shift runs. Running is not free: it drains the AP orb on the party card, at about a minute and a half of running for a full meter. Walking puts AP back slowly and standing still puts it back much faster, so a sprint is something you spend rather than something you hold down. You are never stopped from running, the meter is a cost and not a gate, but AP is the same resource your battle skills are paid with, so arriving at a fight out of breath is a real decision. Facing something and pressing Z acts on it: talking to a person, opening a door, reading a sign, picking up what is on the ground, using a workbench. Facing a party member and pressing Z opens their Empathize sheet. C is a kick. It always kicks with the foot, whatever weapon you are holding. Kicking is how you break crates and barrels, force a door, or shove a movable object; an event that cannot be kicked makes no sound at all, so silence means "this is not a thing to kick". A door named as locked takes between seven and fifteen kicks. If the thing you kick has a wall behind it, it is thrown behind you instead.

controls_menu_hotkeys.title: Controls: Menu Hotkeys
controls_menu_hotkeys.description: Tab opens and closes the menu. Every screen in the game also has a letter of its own that opens it directly from the map, laid out for the muscle memory of a first person RPG: - I Inventory (the backpack) - C Character (the status sheet) - O Outfit (equip) - U Magic and spells - R Rest (the wait and sleep menu) - J Journal (the quest log) - M Map (the minimap toggle) - B Build (furniture and structures) - V Vehicles - F Factions - K Cooking - H Help, which is this book - N Training - Y Bestiary - G Sandbox, which only appears in tester builds Assets, Biologics and Options gave up their letters to Help, Magic and Outfit, so they open from the menu instead. Inside the menu, 1, 2 and 3 open the Thinker, Multiplayer and the Hypernet. On the map those same digit keys, 1 to 9, use the favourite items on your quick bar instead. W, A, S and D move, Z and X are confirm and cancel, Q and E zoom the world map, and T switches between the world map and the local map, so none of those letters can be taken by a menu. F9 quicksaves and F10 quickloads. F11 toggles fullscreen.

controls_mouse.title: Controls: Mouse
controls_mouse.description: The mouse does not move your character. Click and drag anywhere to pan the camera, and it snaps back to you as soon as you move with the keyboard. The wheel zooms, but only on the world map, where + and - do the same thing. Hovering an event on the map labels it, one at a time. In battle, left clicking an enemy performs the currently selected command on it, right clicking cycles to the next command, and the wheel scrolls through the command list. Number keys 1 to 5 pick and fire the matching command. Every menu in the game is a real page: clicking a tab, a row or a button works exactly as you would expect, and the wheel scrolls whichever pane the cursor is sitting over.

controls_controller.title: Controls: Controller
controls_controller.description: A controller is supported everywhere, including the DOM menus, the star map and the 3D minigames. The left stick moves and navigates lists. The right stick pans the camera on the map, the twin of click and drag, and scrolls whatever pane a menu is reading, the twin of the wheel; clicking it (R3) labels every event on screen. L2 and R2 zoom on the world map. L1 and R1 are the page keys: in a menu with tabs they cycle the tabs from anywhere on the page, and in menus with a party switcher they change the character being looked at. On the map they arm the quick bar and step through its filled slots. Anything a keyboard can do a pad can do, with one exception: opening a search field is a click. The magnifier handle is deliberately not focusable so that a pad walking a list can never land inside a text box.

controls_remapping.title: Controls: Remapping
controls_remapping.description: Options has a Commands page where the keyboard and the gamepad are remapped separately. Every default command can be rebound, and so can the extra ones this game adds: Zoom In (Q, LB), Zoom Out (E, RB), Kick (C, RT) and Run (Shift, LT). Bindings are saved with your settings and survive between sessions, so this is worth doing once rather than living with a key that fights your hands.

what_is_on_the_screen.title: What Is On The Screen
what_is_on_the_screen.description: The party HUD sits in the top left corner, on the map and in battle alike. Each member is a row: their name and level, an HP bar with the number written inside it, the AP orb, and an MP bar. There is no portrait, because on the map they are standing right there and in battle the acting member's card is lit and carries a caret. To the right of each card runs a column of chips, and what they carry depends on where you are: - On the map, urgent needs: hunger, sleep, hygiene, cravings, illness. - In battle, stat changes ("STR 1.4x"), class resources (pins, combo, chi) and the states in force. - Statuses show in both places. A chip appears when something needs seeing to, in one colour below the warning line and a louder one below the critical line. While the party is riding, the vehicle stands above the crew as a row of its own, with its condition as an HP bar and its fuel where a member's magic would be. The quick bar sits at the bottom centre: your favourite items on the map, the acting member's skills in battle. Notifications appear at the top left as small parchment cards. Some are transient and some are standing: a standing one (overencumbered, hunted, poisoned) stays up for exactly as long as it is true. The HUD can be turned off in Options, Video, or on the first step of character creation.

searching_inside_menus.title: Searching Inside Menus
searching_inside_menus.description: Every long list in the game wears the same search strip, this book included. It starts collapsed as a small magnifier at the top of the page; click it and a field appears with the caret already in it. While you are typing, the field owns the keyboard: none of the menu hotkeys fire, so writing "ice" cannot open the inventory halfway through the word. Escape empties the field, and Escape again leaves it. Closing the magnifier throws the query away, so a page can never stay quietly filtered behind a handle that gives no sign of it. The main menu has a search of its own that goes wider than one screen: it finds items you carry, gear a companion is wearing, skills (one row per member who knows them), recipes you could make right now with what is in the sack, and creatures in the bestiary, all at once.

saving,_autosave_and_quicksaves.title: Saving, Autosave and Quicksaves
saving,_autosave_and_quicksaves.description: The game autosaves when you change map, at most once every few minutes. That save is a real slot, so a crash or a bad decision costs you a map transition at worst. F9 quicksaves and F10 quickloads. Quicksaves rotate over three dedicated slots instead of writing over each other, so one bad quicksave never destroys the two before it. Any playthrough may overwrite any quicksave. A savegame is smaller than it looks, because most of what you would call "the world" is not in it. See the page on Worlds: the history, the people, the chests, the crops and the market prices belong to the world folder and are shared by every savegame made in that world. A permadeath run whose savegame is deleted still leaves its diary standing in the world folder for whoever plays there next.

worlds_and_savegames.title: Worlds and Savegames
worlds_and_savegames.description: A world is a folder, in the manner of Dwarf Fortress, and several worlds sit side by side on your machine. You make one from the Worlds screen on the title menu; until you do, there is no world and the Explore, Reconnect, Story Mode and Sandbox entries stay greyed out. The world is generated once, up front, not piecemeal as you explore it: the century of history, the people and where they live and work, the shop rotas, the dungeon layout, the politics, the factions' accords, the settlement web, the continental epidemics. What lives in the world rather than in your savegame: - the history and the news, the NPCs and what they think of everyone - artifacts, the dungeon layout, lit torches and bashed doors - what every chest holds and which chests stand open - crops in the ground, livestock, beehives, brewing barrels - shop shelves and market prices, rented rooms, property - the bestiary, the containers, the furniture you have built So a chest emptied by one savegame is empty for all of them, and a second playthrough in the same world walks into a place the first one has already changed. The world clock is monotonic: loading any save continues at the latest date any savegame of that world has reached. Switches are shared by the world by default. Variables are private to your savegame unless the world's manifest names them as shared. Other playthroughs of the same world are in it too: where each one was last saved and who was in it, so a savegame that walks into that place finds them standing there as people.

options.title: Options
options.description: Options is split into tabs, and plugins add their own rows to them rather than growing menus of their own. What is worth knowing is in here: - Video: resolution and fullscreen, pixel perfect scaling, the retro shader, UI and font scaling, whether the party HUD is drawn. - Audio: volumes, shown as percentages, and the battle music picker. - Gameplay: party formation (Close or Loose), the auto idle explorer, world map hints. - Commands: keyboard and gamepad remapping, separately. - Experimental: among other things, the local language model that can write NPC dialogue in place of the Markov chains. Fullscreen turns itself on the first time a distributed build runs; after that your own choice is honoured.

mods_and_updates.title: Mods and Updates
mods_and_updates.description: The game reads a mods folder next to the executable, in the manner of RimWorld. Each subfolder is one mod and mirrors the game's own folder structure, so a mod can replace a data file, add a picture, or ship entirely new content. In the Mod Manager, Enter toggles a mod on and off and the arrows move it up and down the load order; mods at the BOTTOM load last and win. Mods need the desktop build. The title screen carries an UPDATES entry. It reads the public build history, compares the files you have against the ones the build wants, and downloads only what really differs. Nothing is ever moved into place until every file has been downloaded and checked, the files it replaces are backed up first, and the game has to be closed and reopened for the new files to load. There are two channels, STABLE and UNSTABLE, and you can drop back to any earlier build. A build marked as a major update cannot be patched across: the screen will say so and offer the whole game instead.

the_party.title: The Party
the_party.description: The party is at most three people. The first of them is the leader: the one you are actually steering, the one whose needs drain fastest, and the one the world reacts to first. A fourth companion can walk with you without being one of the three. Pets, followers and children trail the party on the map, never join a battle, and can never be hurt or targeted. That slot is explained on its own page. Party members are individuals rather than statistics. Each has their own opinion of every person you meet, their own needs, their own reputation, their own specializations and their own relationships with the other two. Almost nothing in this game is "the party's": it is somebody's. Formation is an option, Close or Loose, and Loose is the default. - Close is the marching column: everyone walks in the leader's footsteps. - Loose cuts the rope. The others keep you company rather than following you, find their own way round the terrain, and only come back once they have been carried off the screen entirely. A loose party lives its own life. Between walks they take up an activity: they stand and think, go and look at something, walk up to a townsperson and hold a conversation, or talk to each other. They look after themselves too: a meter under 35% sends that member off to eat, to wash, to find a piano or an arcade cabinet, to talk to somebody, or to rent a room for the night out of the party purse, which then opens for everybody. Everything they do is announced, because it happens while you are looking somewhere else. Running for two full seconds calls them in and forms the column for as long as you keep running. Walking never does. Stand facing a companion and press confirm to open their Empathize sheet.

making_your_characters.title: Making Your Characters
making_your_characters.description: Characters are built one at a time, and there are three ways to build one. - Quick walks the wizard's steps: look, class, traits, gear. - Dossiers are pre-made characters. Some are endless and can be taken again in any world; the rest are spent once used. A dossier can carry its own vehicle, parked ready for it, its own procedural background and hometown, and alternate skins to be played in. - Detailed hands the character to the Empathize panel with a Create tab, where every field of the sheet is editable: humanoid or creature, name, gender, class, level, portrait, sprite, age, nation of birth, traits, specializations, personality, ideology, faction, wealth, morality, romantic and sexual orientation, reproduction, and a reroll of the backstory. Whichever route you take, closing the sheet returns you to the prompt for the next member, so the party is built one person at a time. Starting gear is chosen by PRICE, never by power: the starter weapon pool is the cheapest weapon of each type in the game, and a class loadout has to fit a fixed budget. Anything a trait hands you is separate and is exactly what the trait says.

classes.title: Classes
classes.description: A class decides three things: your starting numbers, which schools of skill you learn fastest, and an element you lean toward. Every class names a primary and a secondary set of skill categories. Those are not a restriction on what you can do, they are what you are good at learning: - Primary categories earn progression three times as fast, and cost half as much knowledge to buy from. - Secondary categories earn one and a half times as fast, at full price. - A category outside your curriculum can only be entered once you already know something in it, gives you no free way in, and charges three times over. The Training encyclopedia only lists your own curriculum, so a Knight is never offered Necromancy on the shelf. That is a display rule, not a wall: the spell is still learnable the hard way. Class no longer decides what you may hold. Any class can equip any weapon; how well it is wielded is a trainable proficiency instead. See the equipment pages. Creature classes are a separate set (Feral, Mimic, Monster, Mana Cyborg, Ghost, Zombie, Mutant, Drone). A character on a creature class is not a person shaped like an animal, they are an animal.

traits.title: Traits
traits.description: Traits are bought with a purse of trait points at creation. Every trait carries a cost: a positive one is paid for, and a NEGATIVE one is a drawback that pays points back into the purse, so taking a flaw is how you afford a virtue. Traits change base stats, hand out skills, items and equipment, and they are read all over the game long after creation: - Whether an NPC likes you at all: compatible traits are worth a standing bonus and incompatible ones a penalty, before anything is even said. - How much anybody minds the state you are in. A Germaphobe reacts to an unwashed traveller nearly three times as hard as an ordinary person, and somebody Feral does not register it at all. - Which specializations you begin with a head start in. - What your companions do with their spare time and what they say while doing it. A trait is a permanent fact about that character, not a slot to be reshuffled.

attributes.title: Attributes
attributes.description: Six attributes describe a body and a mind: - STR, what you can lift and how hard a blow lands. - CON, how much punishment the body absorbs, and how long it holds a choke. - DEX, speed and precision, evasion, and how hard you are to take hold of. - INT, learning and the mathematical schools of magic. - WIS, judgement, resistance and the intuitive schools. - PSI, the one people call luck. It moves how enemies react to being talked to, what turns up in loot, and how often the world quietly decides in your favour. Attributes are shown as medallions on the status sheet along with whatever is currently modifying them. In battle the HUD shows the modifier as a plain multiplier ("STR 1.4x") rather than as arrows, because what matters is where the number ended up.

playing_a_creature.title: Playing A Creature
playing_a_creature.description: A party member does not have to be a person. The creature builder mints one from an archetype (or two archetypes crossed together), a battler and a sprite, and the resulting body is a real body: the limb and organ system reads its archetype, so a creature has the parts that species has, with the reach, the number of hands and the vulnerabilities that follow. A creature on one of the creature classes is non-sentient. It holds no conversation, takes no political side, saves for nothing and owns nothing. A creature on a civilised class is a person who happens to be shaped like an animal, and is treated as one everywhere in the game. Anatomy is not cosmetic. How many weapons you can hold, whether you can hold one at all, whether you can be choked, and what a pregnancy produces are all read off the archetype.

portraits_and_3d_models.title: Portraits and 3D Models
portraits_and_3d_models.description: Each character is drawn in exactly one of three ways, chosen at creation and never mixed: - A bust: a hand drawn portrait. - A model: a procedural 3D body sculpted in the creation wizard. Six anatomical slots (head, torso, two arms, two legs) can each be filled with the matching part of any registered creature, so a dragon head over a human torso on spider legs is a legal character. Height, build, head size, ears, nose and skin are sliders; fangs, horns, tail, wings and halo are toggles. - A sprite: this marks a monster, a creature built on an existing species, an enemy recruited by talking, or a summon. Those are always shown as the procedural 3D model of their species. Whatever you choose is what the status screen, the dialogue busts and the Empathize panel all use.

recruiting_people.title: Recruiting People
recruiting_people.description: Anybody you meet can end up in the party. There are three routes in: - Talking a monster round in battle, which is its own page. - Asking a townsperson through the Empathize panel, once they think well enough of the member doing the asking. - Adopting a creature as a pet or follower, and later training it up. A recruited townsperson stops being scenery: their event is removed from the map and their whole profile, personality, traits, skills, wealth, history, is carried into the party actor. Their standing with everyone else comes with them. The party is three. Somebody has to leave for somebody to join. Retired members are not deleted: they are put back on the dossier board and can be recalled later, which is also how a party rebuilds after a disaster.

pets,_followers_and_children.title: Pets, Followers and Children
pets,_followers_and_children.description: A fourth companion trails the party without being a party member. It never fights, cannot die, and cannot be targeted by anything. - A creature recruited from a monster that talks is a follower. - One recruited from a monster that does not is a pet. The difference is purely what the menus call it. - A child is whatever a pregnancy produced. It wears the sprite of the parent who bore it and carries a generated name. Only one of them walks with you at a time, but every one you have ever taken in is kept on the Followers page, where the leash can be handed over or the animal released. A pet or a follower can be TRAINED into a real party member. What it can be trained AS comes off its species roster: something that talks is never drilled into one of the beast classes, and a species that supports nothing falls back to Beast, or to Freelancer for somebody who talks. Training is measured in world clock minutes, which only move when you do, so it is paid for in steps walked and hours waited. Animal Training (or Leadership, for a follower who talks) takes days off the total. Only the companion actually walking with you makes progress. Children are family and are never trained; a summon is not yours to train either.

reproduction_and_pregnancy.title: Reproduction and Pregnancy
reproduction_and_pregnancy.description: Every body has a reproductive type, chosen at creation and drawn from the species. There are five: - Testicles. Fertility, sperm count, motility and morphology are simulated and answer to hormones and to the state of the body. - Uterus. A 28 day cycle runs continuously, with the fertile window on days 12 to 16 of it. The Biologics screen shows the day of the cycle and whether it is fertile right now. - Oviparous. A clutch of one to four eggs develops instead of a single offspring. - Plant. Seeds develop one after another and the cycle never ends: a seed is produced, the term restarts, and the stockpile grows until the seeds are planted. - Mitosis. The body divides, and what comes out is another of you. A pregnancy runs for the term of the SPECIES, not a fixed number of days, and its progress is written into the Biologics screen: gestational age, the stage the fetus has reached, and the ordinary miseries of it, which arrive as real states rather than as text. Heart rate rises. Being pregnant is felt. What is born is a person the party now travels with: it is registered as a child in the Followers menu, with its own name and its parent's face. A clutch of eggs registers every hatchling. Mitosis is the exception and produces a copy rather than a child. The whole thing is written into the party diary as it happens: the pregnancy beginning, the birth, the split.

death,_gravestones_and_permadeath.title: Death, Gravestones and Permadeath
death,_gravestones_and_permadeath.description: Falling in battle is not automatically the end. Health protection and the danger warnings give you a chance to break off a fight that is going wrong, and fleeing is always allowed and always works. When a character does die, they leave a gravestone where it happened. The grave is a real place in the world: it stays on the map, it can be found again by anybody playing that world, and it is what a restoration is performed on. Permadeath is the harder setting: the character is gone, their quicksaves go with them, and their diary stays standing in the world folder for whoever plays there next to read. A party wiped out is not the end of the world either, only of that party: the world keeps its history, its people and its changed chests, and the next party walks into what the last one left behind. Losing a limb is not death and is not undone by a heal. See the pages on the body.

what_your_companions_say.title: What Your Companions Say
what_your_companions_say.description: Two or more companions talk to each other. A discussion is two to four beats, each one line, chosen from what is actually happening: - something that just happened and has not been discussed yet, chiefly a purchase - everybody under 40% health, which they will mention - one of them with a meter under 35%, which becomes the subject - a line out of the party diary from the last few hours: the fight won, the artifact found, the floor gone down, the person who joined - where they are standing, by family of biome rather than by exact biome - the road, the money, the leader, the plan - one of their own personalities opening and another answering The last word is often a closer out of a third member's personality, which is what makes the same script read differently depending on who is standing in it. The same purchase gets three different opinions: the disciplined one resents the expense, the hedonistic one asks why only one was bought, the cautious one asks what the party is now short of. They talk while driving too, with the bubbles over the vehicle, and in the train, the coach and the taxi. A party of one has nobody to talk to and falls back to talking to themselves.

the_auto_explorer.title: The Auto Explorer
the_auto_explorer.description: There is an option that lets the game play itself while you are not touching it. The party explores on its own, picks its way across the map, and behaves much as a loose companion does: seeing to its own needs, talking to people, and getting on with things. It is a comfort feature, not a cheat: it takes the same steps you would take and pays the same costs, and it hands control back the moment you press anything.

levels_and_experience.title: Levels and Experience
levels_and_experience.description: Experience is earned by winning fights, and a level raises the six attributes and the two pools, HP and MP. Levels are not the whole of progress, and in this game they are not even most of it. What actually changes what a character can do is: - what skills they have been taught, which costs knowledge and not experience - how far their specializations have been trained, which costs use - what they are carrying, and how well they are trained to carry it - what condition their body is in A high level character with an untrained weapon and a broken arm will lose to a low level one who has trained the weapon and is whole.

knowledge_points.title: Knowledge Points
knowledge_points.description: Knowledge (KP) is the currency skills are bought with, and it belongs to the party rather than to one member. It is earned by: - winning fights, scaled by how dangerous the enemies were against the party's median level, so grinding things far beneath you pays almost nothing - finishing quests - resolving a procedural adventure well - what is learned in dreams - scanning objects with the Raman spectroscope What a skill costs to teach is what it is worth in a fight, not a flat fee. The MP and AP it asks for is read first, then damage scaling, flat damage, repeats, how many it hits, and what it inflicts. The plainest working in the book costs 50 KP, an ordinary one a few hundred, the strongest ordinary one a couple of thousand. An Esoteric working costs ten times its score, and a Forbidden one a hundred times. A primary school halves the price, a secondary school pays full, an outside school triples it, and nothing is ever cheaper than 50 KP.

the_atlas_of_circles.title: The Atlas of Circles
the_atlas_of_circles.description: Skills are not a shopping list, they are a sphere grid. Each school is drawn as an alchemical circle: concentric rings running from the school's weakest working outward to its strongest, joined by short spokes, with upgrade spurs hanging off the rim that dead end in its esoteric workings. You may only buy a skill you are standing next to. ONE known neighbour is enough, links are alternative ways in and never joint requirements, and the innermost ring of a school is always open, so a pupil who knows nothing still has a way in. Forbidden workings are not on the grid at all. They sit alone in the heart of the figure, joined to nothing and to each other least of all: the whole school must be known before any of them opens, and then any one of them may be taken first. One school is drawn at a time. The pager on the header bar changes school, or walk off the rim to left or right. The wheel and Shift zoom, dragging pans, and choosing a skill opens its sheet over the circle.

training_and_progression.title: Training and Progression
training_and_progression.description: Each party member can be training one skill at a time, tracked separately per person. Progress comes from: - winning a battle, worth 3 points to each member - using a skill of the same category in battle, worth 2 points Primary categories multiply that by three and secondary categories by one and a half, which is what makes a class feel like a class.

specializations.title: Specializations
specializations.description: There are around eight hundred real world specializations, from Wrestling to Accounting to Beekeeping, each governed by one attribute and each with five tiers: Untrained, Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced, Master. A specialization's level is the highest of three things: what has been trained through play, what the class grants as a head start, and what a trait grants. So changing class or taking a trait shows up on the sheet at once, without any seeding step. They train by DOING, not by spending. Cook and your cooking rises, wrestle and your wrestling rises, sell and your haggling rises. The leader earns full value; anybody else present earns 35%. The first tier costs three points. They are read everywhere. A specialization decides how well you forge, whether a lock opens, how much a hold hurts, what a merchant will accept, and whether you can read a recipe at all.

class_passives.title: Class Passives
class_passives.description: Every class carries signature passives that need no slot and no activation. Some are combat abilities and some only matter outside a fight. They are the reason two characters of the same level with the same gear do not play the same, and they are listed on the status sheet under Passives so you can read exactly what your class is quietly doing for you.

the_nine_skill_slots.title: The Nine Skill Slots
the_nine_skill_slots.description: A character may know hundreds of workings and can take NINE of them into a fight. The skill menu is tabbed by role and the nine chosen are the ones drawn on the battle quick bar. This is the loadout decision of the game. Everything you know is always yours; what you have READY is what you have prepared for the next fight, and changing it is free between fights.

fusing_spells.title: Fusing Spells
fusing_spells.description: From the Magic page, two workings can be forged into a new one. - The DOMINANT slot takes a spell you know and decides how the result behaves: its damage, its scope, its hit type, its icon. - The RECESSIVE slot takes a spell OR a skill. If it is a skill, the result is a skill; otherwise it stays magic. - Any named animation can be chosen for it, previewable in 3D. The fused ability costs the SUM of its parts in MP and AP, and forging is paid in knowledge, the sum of what teaching the components would have cost. The components are FORGOTTEN when fused, and the fusion can be split back into them at any time.

grimoires_and_skill_books.title: Grimoires and Skill Books
grimoires_and_skill_books.description: A grimoire is a book that offers five random workings and lets one reader claim one of them. The five are rolled once when the book is opened, against the whole party, and do not change: switching reader does not reroll them. A reader can only claim an offer whose MP cost fits inside their maximum MP and that they do not already know. The rest are greyed out. The party's median PSI raises the rare chance that a Forbidden working surfaces among the five. There are variants: a school specific grimoire, a category specific skill book, and the Forbidden Grimoire, which offers nothing else.

blade_seeds.title: Blade Seeds
blade_seeds.description: There are twelve seeds, one per weapon type. A seed is a slow, permanent upgrade path for a whole class of weapon rather than for a single sword: it grows as that weapon type is used and what it grows into is procedural, so two worlds do not grow the same blade. A seed is a long term investment in a way of fighting, and it survives the weapon that carried it.

equipment_hands_and_slots.title: Equipment: Hands and Slots
equipment_hands_and_slots.description: The equipment system does not have a dual wield flag. It has ANATOMY. Every body part that can hold a weapon, as declared by the species, IS a weapon slot. A hand takes a weapon or a shield without distinction, so two shields are as legal as two swords. - A two handed weapon needs two free hands. With one hand you may carry one one handed weapon or one shield, and no other weapon slot exists at all. - A body with no hands holds its weapon in its MOUTH: one slot, and it takes anything, one handed or two handed, weapon or shield. A class tagged for it, the samurai, keeps that mouth slot on top of its hands. - Eight weapon slots is the ceiling, however many limbs a body grows. - Past two weapons the arsenal stops being a sum: each parameter becomes the MEDIAN of what is carried, and two of them, drawn at random, are the ones that swing each turn. Six swords is not six swords of damage. - Losing a limb takes its slot with it and hands back whatever it was holding.

weapon_proficiency.title: Weapon Proficiency
weapon_proficiency.description: Any class can equip any weapon type. Classes no longer lock weapons. How well a weapon is used is a trainable specialization, one per weapon type, twelve in all. It starts at Intermediate for the types your class used to be limited to, and Untrained for everything else, and it scales the weapon's own parameters: - Untrained 33% - Beginner 67% - Intermediate 100% - Advanced 110% - Master 125% Winning a battle grants one proficiency point per equipped weapon type, so an untrained weapon carried long enough catches up with a class issued one, and past Intermediate it overtakes it. An exotic weapon is worth picking up early precisely because carrying it is how it becomes good.

what_a_weapon_scales_on.title: What a Weapon Scales On
what_a_weapon_scales_on.description: A weapon does not always swing on STR. Its attack skill decides which attribute it reads, and the equip screen names it when the weapon slot is selected: - no attack skill: STR - otherwise one of DEX, INT, WIS, CON, PSI, or a mix of two This is why a wand in the hands of a strong fool is a stick, and why a knife can be a DEX weapon and a club a CON one. Read the scaling line before judging a weapon by its attack number.

armour_and_derived_stats.title: Armour and Derived Stats
armour_and_derived_stats.description: Beyond defence, what you wear feeds four social and practical stats: - Clothes: Substance and Stealth - Robes: Arcane - Light armour: Stealth - Heavy armour: Intimidation Weapons feed them too: daggers and bows give Stealth, swords, heavy weapons, axes and claws give Intimidation, staves give Arcane, whips, projectiles and guns give Substance. These are read outside combat. What you are dressed as changes how people answer you, what a guard assumes, and which approaches are open to you at all. Turning up to a negotiation in full plate is a decision, not a detail.

modifiers_on_gear.title: Modifiers on Gear
modifiers_on_gear.description: A weapon or a piece of armour can carry a modifier that changes its stats, its price and its traits: - Sharp raises STR and the price. Weapons only. - Refined raises CON and WIS and the price. Anything. - Poisoned adds poison and changes the price. Weapons only. - Worn lowers CON and WIS and the price. Armour only. Modifiers are part of the item, so a modified piece is worth looking at even when its base is humble.

weight_and_encumbrance.title: Weight and Encumbrance
weight_and_encumbrance.description: Everything you carry has a weight and the party has a carry capacity. Go over it and a standing notification appears and stays up for exactly as long as you are overloaded. Weight is why containers matter, why a camper with a hold is worth having, and why the answer to a rich dungeon is often two trips.

the_backpack.title: The Backpack
the_backpack.description: The backpack is tabbed by category: food, medical, tools, weapons, armour, materials. It carries the weight readout, the item detail card, and the favourites bar. Nine favourite slots hold usable items and are drawn on the same quick bar the battle system puts skills on. On the map, keys 1 to 9 use the item in that slot outright; an item that has to be given to somebody asks who, right there over the map. In the backpack the same keys assign the inspected item to a slot, items can be dragged onto slots, and right clicking clears one. Only usable items qualify. Weapons and armour are equipped, not favourited.

artifacts.title: Artifacts
artifacts.description: Artifacts are procedurally generated items, weapons and armour: named, unique, and belonging to the world rather than to your savegame, so an artifact one party leaves behind is the same artifact another party finds. They can be analysed on the Hypernet with the Artifact Analyzer, which is how you learn what an unfamiliar one actually does rather than guessing from its name.

containers_and_storage.title: Containers and Storage
containers_and_storage.description: Chests, cupboards, crates and sacks all hold things, and what they hold belongs to the world: a chest emptied by one savegame is empty for every other savegame of that world, and which chests stand open is remembered too. The party's own bags are different and stay yours: the extradimensional container, and the holds of the camper and the car. Those travel with you and are the practical answer to weight.

loot_and_rarity.title: Loot and Rarity
loot_and_rarity.description: Random loot is scaled against the party's MEDIAN level, not the leader's, so dragging one high level companion around does not enrich the whole game. Items are named in their rarity colour wherever they appear: in the reward popup, in the backpack, on the shop counter. A haul of several things holds its popup on screen longer so it can actually be read. Every item description in the game is combinatorial, written as a set of alternatives and resolved from the world seed. The same sword reads the same way all through one world, and differently in the next.

the_five_needs.title: The Five Needs
the_five_needs.description: Everybody in this world, your party and every townsperson alike, carries five meters: - Hunger - Sleep - Hygiene - Company (how long since anybody talked to them) - Fun They all run from 100 down to 0 and they all drain as time passes. Time passes when you walk: one minute per ten steps on an ordinary map, ten minutes per tile on the world map, and two minutes per tile in a vehicle. The leader's meters drain fastest, because the leader is the one doing the walking. Running drains everything faster. They are shown as chips beside each party card on the map, in one colour under 20% and a louder one at 0. The main menu draws them in full, and every change is announced as a popup with the party median, so a change always reads the same way: "Fun 62% up +8". Below 20% is low. At 0 it stops being an inconvenience: hunger at 0 drains HP, sleep at 0 drains MP, and the rest cost you socially and mentally. An augment can slow a need, stop it dead, or reverse it. A ruminant stomach burns less, a somnologic regulator never gets tired, a self cleaning dermis actually GAINS hygiene as you walk.

hunger_and_nutrition.title: Hunger and Nutrition
hunger_and_nutrition.description: Food is not a single number. Every edible thing carries calories, fat and protein, and eating credits all three: what a meal is worth depends on what it is made of, not on its price. The hunger meter can go ABOVE 100. Eating past full takes you up to a ceiling of 150%, and past 110% you are overfed, which is a real state with real penalties. Hunger also burns three times faster while you are over 100, so overeating is not free storage. Temperature stresses the body at both ends. Cold burns extra calories to keep you warm and heat raises your metabolism, so hunger drains faster in bad weather. The travel card shows the ambient temperature and how much it is costing you. At 0 hunger you take continuous HP damage until you eat. Food is bought, foraged, grown, hunted and cooked. The cooking bench combines ingredients into meals whose nutrition is the sum of what went in, so cooking is worth doing for reasons beyond flavour.

sleep,_rest_and_time_awake.title: Sleep, Rest and Time Awake
sleep,_rest_and_time_awake.description: Two different things are tracked, and confusing them will hurt you. The SLEEP METER answers how tired you feel, and a coffee or a sit down refills it. At 0 it drains MP. TIME SINCE YOU LAST ACTUALLY SLEPT is a separate stamp on the world clock, and nothing refills it but a real night's rest. That is the number that turns a dream hellish and starts pulling the party's mind apart. It reads as zero up to a day awake, climbs through two days, and is at maximum at a week, which is where a dream stops being a dream. Beds, campfires, tents and world map camps open the rest menu, where Sleep refills the meter completely whatever hour you choose to wake at. The Wait entry on the menu, and the T hotkey, only run the clock forward and never rest the party: waiting is not sleeping. Cryogenic sleep is a third thing entirely: you pick a YEAR to wake up in, and the world moves on without you. A long rest sometimes drops the party into a dream, which is a place rather than a cutscene. See the dream page.

hygiene,_and_what_it_costs_you.title: Hygiene, and What It Costs You
hygiene,_and_what_it_costs_you.description: Hygiene drains a little faster than sleep does. It is refilled at a washroom, a bathroom, a shower, a sink or a fountain, and loose party members will go and find one on their own when theirs falls under 35%. Here is the part the game never says out loud: HOW CLEAN YOU ARE CHANGES WHAT PEOPLE THINK OF YOU. Standing close enough to talk to somebody means smelling them, so the state of BOTH bodies moves the conversation. Your hygiene is read against the person you are talking to, and their hygiene is read against you: recoiling from somebody costs you a conversation exactly as much as being recoiled from does. The rule is simple. At 60% and above, nobody notices anything. Below that, every single point costs you a little under half a point of standing, and the total penalty is capped at 45 points of opinion, which is enough to turn a friend into a stranger. Traits decide how much anybody minds. Somebody Feral does not register it at all, an Ascetic barely does, a Street Urchin, a Cave Dweller, a Survivalist, a Farmer or a Veteran have all smelled worse for longer. On the other side, the Proud, the Wealthy, the Beautiful, the Perfectionist, the Noble, the Hypochondriac and above all the Germaphobe mind it enormously; a Germaphobe reacts nearly three times as hard as an ordinary person. Several such traits multiply together, and a single "does not notice" trait wins outright. It is felt hardest when courting. A romantic approach reads the same two bodies a SECOND time, at its own heavier weight, on top of the standing it has already dulled, and the panel will tell you which of the two of you needs a bath before you try again. So: wash before a negotiation, before asking somebody to join you, and especially before asking somebody out.

company.title: Company
company.description: Company drains like any other need, and it is fed by talking to people. A conversation with a townsperson feeds it, and so does a conversation between two of your own. A member starved of company will, if the party is loose, walk up to somebody and start a conversation without being told to. That conversation is real: it moves what the other person thinks of THAT member, up or down, and how they both smell is part of it. Gaining standing with somebody feeds the social meter of the member who gained it, which is the quiet reason that being liked is worth something mechanically and not only narratively.

fun.title: Fun
fun.description: Fun is fed by playing: an arcade cabinet, a piano, a pool table, a card game, a good joke landing in conversation. It is announced like any other need, and a joke that lands actually leaves the other person measurably less bored for the rest of the day, because their own Fun meter went up too. A party that never plays anything will drag its Fun to the floor and start complaining about it in banter, which is the game telling you to go and do something pointless for half an hour.

cravings_and_withdrawal.title: Cravings and Withdrawal
cravings_and_withdrawal.description: Five traits are dependencies rather than appetites: alcohol, caffeine, nicotine, narcotics and gambling. Only a member carrying one of those traits keeps a craving meter, so a clean party never shows a single craving bar. A craving is a need read backwards. It CLIMBS while it goes unfed; 0 is somebody who has just had their fix and 100 is somebody in withdrawal. Feeding it drops it straight back to zero. Withdrawal bites at a full meter and does not let go until the craving has been brought back down well below it, so one puff cannot flick it off again. The body still wants it while asleep, only more quietly. Cravings are personal and climb on the member who carries the trait, not on the leader.

limbs_and_organs.title: Limbs and Organs
limbs_and_organs.description: A body is not a single HP bar. Every character and every monster has individual limbs and organs, each with its own health, drawn from its species archetype. Damage is distributed to parts. A part taken to 0 is destroyed, which carries a permanent penalty for as long as it stays that way, and destroyed parts change what you can DO: - A lost hand takes its weapon slot with it and hands back what it was holding. - A body with no hands holds a weapon in its mouth instead. - Damaged legs cost you movement and evasion. - Vital organs are protected from ordinary damage, and are only exposed by deliberate targeting or by a state that opens them. A part at 0 HP, marked damaged, or severed can neither take hold of anything nor be taken hold of, on either side of a fight. Body parts do not come back on their own. They are healed at a clinic, restored by the right magic, or replaced with a prosthetic. In Blood and Oil mode a slashing blow can take a part off the body outright, carrying whatever augment was in it, and a part that cannot come off at all is ruined for good. Anything merely broken still mends under a potion or a spell, in every mode. The status sheet has an Anatomy section that draws the whole body and the condition of every piece of it.

biologics.title: Biologics
biologics.description: Biologics is the deep readout: vital signs, hormones, blood chemistry, brain regions and their activity, blood type, the reproductive cycle, and every condition currently acting on the body. It is a real simulation rather than a decorative panel. Heart rate answers to what is happening to you. Hormones answer to sleep, to injury, to pregnancy. Blood type is chosen once, or rolled once from the name, and sticks to that character forever. The Ley Vein system connects it to the limb damage: blockages show up here when the body they belong to has been hurt.

diseases.title: Diseases
diseases.description: There are hundreds of diseases, each with a transmission chance, one or more vectors (airborne, saliva, bite, contact, sexual and others), stat modifiers that apply while you carry it, and often a state that appears only after the carrier has walked a certain number of steps. That delay is the WINDOW PERIOD: you can be carrying something for a long time before it shows. How it spreads: - Between your own party members, rolled once each time you open the pause menu. - Between the party and a townsperson, rolled each time you open their Empathize panel. Talking to sick people is how you get sick. - Venereal diseases NEVER spread by proximity. They pass only between romantic partners. Every NPC in the world carries a deterministic medical history, seeded from the world, with past diseases and lasting conditions such as badly set bones. It is readable on the Health tab of their panel. The Diagnose action examines the whole party and names every illness they carry, including the ones still inside their window period, and it works in battle as well as on the map.

epidemics.title: Epidemics
epidemics.description: Above individual illness sits a continental epidemic model, and it runs whether or not you are looking at it. An outbreak lives in a real town. Each infected town runs its own curve, resolved one whole day at a time at midnight, and exports cases to other towns along real map distance, with the occasional long jump because people travel. Public response builds the longer a town has had it, and that is what eventually breaks the wave. There are two kinds. A MEDICAL outbreak is a pathogen with a real case fatality ratio. A HYSTERIA is not: dancing fever, genital theft panics, phantom gassers. You catch a hysteria by witnessing it and spread it by talking about it. Every world starts with three already burning: one mass hysteria, one ordinary medical outbreak, and one rare and mortal one. Anyone standing in an infected town is exposed, including you. The people around you are drawn from the same local prevalence, so where the outbreak is, the sick really are sick. Outbreaks are felt through the whole simulation: mood, hiring, shop traffic, need drain, and what people gossip about. They also make the news. The Eurodemics observatory on the Hypernet is where you watch all of this from.

clinics,_prosthetics_and_field_surgery.title: Clinics, Prosthetics and Field Surgery
clinics,_prosthetics_and_field_surgery.description: A clinic can install a body part, remove one, replace one, or fit an implant. Installing a part costs a thousand gold per percent of body health it represents, removal costs a hundred, and vital parts cannot be removed at all. An installed part grants its stat bonus, and removing it takes the bonus away again. FIELD SURGERY is the same theatre carried in a rucksack. The party picks a patient AND a surgeon, nothing is bought, only parts already in the pack can be fitted, an augment can be taken OUT but never seated, and no fee is charged. Every operation is a roll and the odds are shown before you take it: - the surgeon's Surgery specialization, 35 / 50 / 65 / 78 / 90 percent by tier - under a roof +10, in a cave -5, in the open -10 - rain -15, a storm -25, snow +5, because cold slows the bleeding - operating on yourself -15 A failure wounds the patient somewhere else. A vital organ is only ever at risk in Blood and Oil mode, and only there can a part leave the body, carrying its augment out with it.

augments.title: Augments
augments.description: The Augments register is its own menu entry and has two lists. - Fitted: every augment the party is actually wearing, named with its wearer and the socket it sits in. - Catalogue: everything that exists, so you can read what an augment does before paying a clinic to graft it in. The dossier on the right says what it costs, what it adds, what skill it teaches (with that skill's own description), and every socket that will take it, including creature sockets, so a dragon's rear left leg is listed alongside the ordinary human ones. Augments are also the way to bend the needs system: the right hardware slows a meter, stops it, or turns it around.

weather,_temperature_and_the_body.title: Weather, Temperature and the Body
weather,_temperature_and_the_body.description: Weather is not scenery. The ambient temperature is a real number, it is shown on the travel card, and it acts on you: - Cold burns calories to keep you warm, so hunger drains faster. - Heat raises your metabolism, which does the same thing. - Rain and storms make field surgery much harder; snow makes it slightly easier. - Weather drives what people do, where they are, and how a settlement feels. Dress and plan for it. A long crossing in bad weather costs food, and food is weight.

how_a_fight_starts.title: How a Fight Starts
how_a_fight_starts.description: There are no random encounters. Every monster you fight is a creature that was standing on the map, that you could see, and that you walked into. Each one carries its level over its head, so you always know what you are about to touch. Once a fight starts, turns are INDIVIDUAL: each battler acts as soon as its own turn comes up, in order of agility, and your action happens immediately after you choose it rather than at the end of a planning phase. There is no round where everyone commits first. Enemies keep their damage between fights. Wound something, run away, come back later and it is still wounded. The bodies of the dead stay on the map as corpses. Fleeing always works. There is no escape roll to fail.

the_battle_commands.title: The Battle Commands
the_battle_commands.description: The command menu holds more than the usual four: - Attack, with whatever is in your hands. What it costs, how far it reaches and what it scales on is the weapon's business. - Guard. - Skills and Magic, holding only the nine you carry. - Item. - Check, which opens the enemy's body: every limb and organ, its condition, and the chance of hitting it. - Target, which aims your next blow at one specific part. - Wrestle, which takes hold of the enemy. It has its own page. - Talk, which is a whole second way of ending a fight. It has its own page too. - Reload, when a firearm is empty. - Escape. Wrestle and Talk are COMMANDS, not skills: they cost no slot in your loadout, cannot be forgotten, and are offered by the body rather than by the class. With the mouse: left click an enemy to run the selected command on it, right click to cycle commands, wheel to scroll them, and keys 1 to 5 for the first five commands.

mp_and_ap.title: MP and AP
mp_and_ap.description: Two resources drive what you can do. MP is magic. Spells cost it, it refills slowly, and it is what most rites and summons are held with. AP is momentum, and it is the one worth understanding. It is spent by skills in battle AND by sprinting on the map, out of the same meter. AP caps at 100. That link is deliberate. Running everywhere means arriving at fights with an empty bar, and standing still is how AP comes back fastest. Walking regenerates it slowly, standing still much faster, and running drains it at about a minute and a half for a full meter. Whether an ability costs MP or AP is decided by what kind of ability it is: magic is written in CamelCase, costs MP and lives under Magic; a skill is written in plain words, costs AP and lives under Skills.

hitting_what_you_aim_at.title: Hitting What You Aim At
hitting_what_you_aim_at.description: Monsters have the same limbs and organs your party does, drawn from their species. The Check command lists every part of the enemy with its condition and the percentage chance of hitting it. Target then aims your next blow at one of them. That chance is built from the part's size, your weapon type read against your own stats, and a random swing of plus or minus ten percent per part. Aiming has two purposes. Destroying a limb takes away what that limb DOES: a monster with a broken leg is slower, one with a ruined wing cannot fly, one with no hands cannot hold its weapon. And vital organs, which ordinary blows are not allowed to reach, ARE reachable with a deliberate targeted attack. That is how a big creature is killed quickly, and it is also how a big creature kills you. Damage to parts persists through the fight, so a destroyed part stays destroyed, and a finishing blow can sever the part outright.

wrestling.title: Wrestling
wrestling.description: Wrestle is offered to any body with at least one limb still whole enough to take hold with, and any enemy still standing to take hold of. It costs nothing and is never learned: it is anatomy, not a skill. Choosing it aims at one enemy, and once that enemy is chosen your command menu is REPLACED by the grapple plan. Three decisions: - which of YOUR limbs takes the hold - which of THEIR limbs it is taken on - which hold to use Each row shows the real odds of it working. A separate window lists the whole body, with the state of every part and a line saying what that limb can do or what taking hold of it will be like. A part at 0 HP, marked damaged, or severed can neither grab nor be grabbed, on either side of the fight. The holds, and what each one reads: - Grapple, STR against DEX. Takes hold. Everything else needs one first. - Strike, STR against DEX. The exception: it needs no hold, and to the head it can concuss. - Joint lock, DEX against STR. Pins, and often breaks the guard. - Wrench, STR against CON. Hurts far more, and can leave them bleeding. - Slam, CON against DEX. The heaviest ordinary hold: guard broken, winded, and a chance to stun. - Choke, CON against CON, on the head only. Guard broken, exposed vitals, and a chance to stun. - Rip, STR against CON. Low odds, enormous damage, and it can tear the limb away outright. Everything is scaled by your Wrestling specialization, which trains by wrestling. And if you have trained ANY martial art, you can finish a hold with that art's real moves without ever having learned them as skills: the finisher shelf lists them with the art they come from and the odds of landing them. Wrestling is how an unarmed character stays dangerous, how a fight is won against something that hits harder than you, and how a limb is taken off a monster deliberately.

talking_to_monsters.title: Talking to Monsters
talking_to_monsters.description: Not every fight has to end in a corpse. A monster tagged as able to understand you can be talked to, and the Talk command opens a panel with the odds of each approach printed beside it. Every enemy carries a DISPOSITION from 1 to 100, rolled when it appears: 40% of monsters start low (10 to 40), 40% middling (41 to 70) and 20% high (71 to 100), shifted by their species. Hurting it lowers its disposition, by between 5 and 15 points depending on how hard you hit it, so a fight you have been winning is a conversation you have been losing. What you can do: - Chat, which builds rapport. Its chance is the enemy's disposition plus one fifth of the difference between your PSI and its own, floored at 10% and capped at 95%. - Ask it to surrender, at the same odds. It flees the fight. - Ask it to join the party, which needs an open slot in your three. Above 80 disposition it uses the ordinary talk chance; below that there is still a small chance, never lower than 5%. - Ask it to follow you, or adopt it as a pet. Something that talks needs 70 disposition before it will consider it; an animal is judged on the ordinary chance. - Insult it, which always lands and always makes things worse. - Throw a stone, which always works on anything. - Pet it. Some creatures are not company. Anything marked as a force rather than a person, the petrodemons above all, refuses every approach with the same answer: no talking round, no petting, no following, no joining. A monster you talk into joining becomes a real party member. One you take as a pet or a follower walks behind you instead, and can be trained into a party member later.

enemy_levels_and_where_they_live.title: Enemy Levels and Where They Live
enemy_levels_and_where_they_live.description: How dangerous a place is depends on the option under Enemy Spawn, and there are three answers. BALANCED. Roaming enemies come out of a band that opens upward from the party's own median level: a party of median level L meets levels L to L + 7 + L/10. A level 1 party meets 1 to 8, a level 50 party meets 50 to 62. Exactly one encounter per world tile is placed above that band as a boss, never over 100. DISTANCE FROM SPAWN, the default. What decides how hard a place is, is the PLACE. The level everything is pitched around comes from how far the world square you are standing on lies from the square you started the game on. Level 1 at home, the top of the roster at the far corner, a smooth climb between. Near where you began the world stays gentle and far from it lethal, whatever level you have reached, so a run is a journey outward rather than a treadmill. A square fields the creatures whose habitat matches the biome and whose level falls in the ten level bracket that place sits in. CHAOS. Nothing is held back and nothing is remembered: the whole roster, flat random, level 1 to 110, redealt every time you enter a map. No creature is exclusive to a country. Every nation holds every creature its biomes hold; the nation only tints how COMMON each of them is, never whether it is there at all. Above all three sits THE CALENDAR, and it cannot be argued with: - 2001: the mode's own band, untouched. - 2002 to 2009: the whole band climbs ten levels a year. - 2010 to 2011: the band is thrown away. Anything from 1 to 110 roams. - 2012 onward: nothing below level 80 is left, and there is no ceiling. The world gets worse. Waiting is not a strategy.

how_monsters_behave.title: How Monsters Behave
how_monsters_behave.description: A roaming monster is not a moving trap. Each one carries a movement personality that decides three separate things: what it does when nothing is happening, how it notices you (sight range, facing cone, line of sight) and what it does once it has. The personalities include: Fixed, Random, Approach, Fleeing, Skittish, Grazer, Sentry, Guard, Patrol, Territorial, Ambusher, Lurker, Mimic, Swooper, Stalker, Hunter, Charger, Pack, Erratic, Drifter, Orbiter, Scavenger and Coward. This is worth reading the map for. A Grazer will not notice you. A Sentry has a cone and can be walked around. An Ambusher is not where it appears to be. A Stalker is already following you. A Pack does not fight alone.

danger_warnings_and_surviving_a_blow.title: Danger Warnings and Surviving a Blow
danger_warnings_and_surviving_a_blow.description: Two things stand between you and a bad decision. Before a fight, the party's median level is compared with what you are about to touch, and a warning is thrown up on the screen when it is out of your league. Enemy levels are drawn over their heads on the map for the same reason. Inside a fight, each character carries ONE health protection charge per battle: the first blow that would kill them leaves them at 1 HP instead. It is spent once and does not come back until the next fight, so it buys you one mistake and not two. In Blood and Oil mode that charge does not exist at all.

difficulty_and_combat_modes.title: Difficulty and Combat Modes
difficulty_and_combat_modes.description: Several settings change what combat IS, most of them chosen at character creation. - PEACEFUL. Monsters do not act unless you hurt them: each turn an unprovoked enemy skips its turn with a line about what it is doing instead. Provocation is per enemy, so untouched monsters keep grazing. A party wipe simply respawns you at your respawn point with nobody dead. Roaming monsters that would chase you wander instead. - ORDINARY. Death leaves a gravestone and the run continues. - HARDCORE and BLOOD AND OIL. Death is terminal: a game over, no respawn, and the character is permanently removed. Blood and Oil also removes the health protection charge, and lets a slashing blow take a body part off outright, carrying its augment with it. A part it only breaks is healed by potions and spells exactly as in every other mode. - CARD COMBAT, which replaces the command menu entirely. See its own page. - MAP BATTLE, which fights on the live map. See its own page.

map_battle_mode.title: Map Battle Mode
map_battle_mode.description: An experimental option turns every fight into a tactical battle on the map you are already standing on, rather than a separate battle screen. - Everyone fights from where they are standing. Whoever bumped the monster holds the tile they bumped it from and every other member keeps the tile they are on. Only somebody off screen is placed, on a muster tile near the fight. - Every other monster on the map stays exactly where it is and keeps its own behaviour. Any of them that wanders within a few tiles JOINS THE FIGHT, with its own HP card and its own slot in the turn order. - A townsperson standing near the brawl joins YOUR side if the party is well liked, or if they are simply brave. They fight from their own profile: their level, their stats, their skills, their pockets. - A Move command lets the acting battler reposition before choosing an action, with a range driven by agility. - Attacks have real reach. Every weapon carries a range: 1 for ordinary melee, 2 for spears, whips, staves and flails, more for bows, guns and thrown weapons, and a clear line of sight is required. Skills carry their own range. - A combatant that steps into water starts swimming by itself, and swimming costs more movement per tile, so a river is a genuine obstacle. The round runs: the party and the troop interleaved by agility, then any townspeople who joined, then the WORLD step, where every roaming monster, every townsperson and your own pet all take exactly one tile at once. Nothing outside the fight moves at any other time, so the map is a still frame while you read, and lurches forward once a round.

card_combat.title: Card Combat
card_combat.description: An alternative combat mode, chosen at character creation or toggled in the experimental options. The running fight keeps the mode it started with; the new setting applies from the next one. - Every party member has their OWN deck, hand and energy, built automatically from that member's class skills. There is no deck builder. - Playing one card IS that member's action for the turn. - Energy replaces MP and AP. A card costs between 1 and 6 energy depending on what the skill would have cost; a basic attack costs 1. - Energy starts at 0 and gains 1 at the start of each of that member's turns, to a cap of 6. Passing the turn grants 2 and draws a card. - The deck holds each skill in copies weighted by cost, so cheap cards come up more often, padded to at least eight with plain attacks. - You hold four cards, draw one a turn, and the opening hand of four always contains something cheap.

summons.title: Summons
summons.description: A summon is a temporary fourth party member. In a fight it exists only for that fight: never saved, never in the menu, gone when the battle ends or when you stop being able to pay for it. What can be called: a creature, a person the party has MARKED, the pet on your leash, a reflection of the summoner, or a revenant, one of the travellers you have lost. Each rite draws only from its own kind, so a demonic rite calls demons and nothing else. A summon is never stronger than the fight. Its numbers are re-cut against the median of your own party and against the level of the troop actually on the field, then multiplied by that rite's share: a familiar is half a traveller, a titan a little more than one. It keeps its SHAPE, so a bruiser is still a bruiser. Two rites are exempt and say so: the petrodemon, which is held by your oil and priced accordingly, and the elder entity, which is balanced against nothing at all, arrives with the numbers it was born with, and drinks the summoner dry in about three turns. What holds a summon there differs by kind: HP for demons, undead, shadows, swarms, titans; MP for elementals, celestials, fae, the void; AP for the reflection; gold for constructs, war machines, dragons, champions; SOUL for spirits; OIL for the petrodemon. Beasts, verdants, familiars and called people simply stay a fixed few turns. When you cannot pay, it leaves. It is never lethal: a summoner who cannot pay in blood is left at 1 HP. THE FAMILIAR is somebody's rather than the party's. Which creature answers is decided by the CLASS of whoever calls it, its name is rolled once out of THEIR name and never changes, and it is measured against their stats and their level alone. Change class and the pact is remade. The first time it is called it joins the Followers page for good. While anything is summoned, a HYPER bar fills with the damage the party deals, one hit contributing at most a third of it. Full, the summon unleashes its ULTIMATE and the bar empties. Which ultimate depends on the party's median level in brackets of ten, growing in damage, widening to the whole enemy line, and adding its own signature effect at higher brackets. Damage is capped as a fraction of each target's maximum HP, so it is a large hit and never a delete button. A summon is always CPU controlled and never gets the 1 HP death protection: when it dies it is gone. OUTSIDE a fight the same rites answer, and what they call walks with you in a trailing slot of its own. Every point of MP paid buys a fixed number of steps, and when the last is walked the binding lets go. It joins any fight you get into, at the stature it was called with.

the_arena.title: The Arena
the_arena.description: The arena is combat for its own sake, in two shapes. - GAUNTLET, a run of fights in a chosen level bracket. - BIOME TRIAL, a run against the fauna of a chosen biome. Whichever party you bring is RESCALED to the bracket, so an arena is a fair test rather than a level check. You can even fight it with a random roster instead of your own. Winning builds a streak, and the streak pays: ascending gold and items the further you get, in the gauntlet and in single arena fights alike. Losing the streak is losing the ladder, not the run.

bullet_hell_sequences.title: Bullet Hell Sequences
bullet_hell_sequences.description: Some fights break into a bullet hell sequence, in the manner of Touhou or Undertale: you steer a small craft, dodge the pattern the enemy is throwing, and shoot back. It is a real part of the fight rather than a minigame on the side. What happens in it is what happens to you.

spirit_battlers.title: Spirit Battlers
spirit_battlers.description: A spirit battler is a fought creature turned into something you can field yourself: defeated enemies join a roster, and one of them can be brought into a fight as a spirit in place of an ordinary battler, at a cost that scales with what it was. It runs on its own switch, so a world where it is not enabled simply fights ordinary battles.

mimicry.title: Mimicry
mimicry.description: The mimic skills copy other bodies, and there are six of them: - Partial mimicry: take the enemy's face and its map sprite. Numbers unchanged. - Full mimicry: take everything. Stats, HP, MP, AP, skills, body archetype and looks. - Mirror: re-execute the last skill the enemy used, against the enemy. - Copy ally: take a companion's name, class, skills, sprite and body. - Random: full mimicry of a creature drawn at random from everything that exists. - Mutation: merge two archetypes at random into your own body parts only. They need exactly one enemy on the field, which is a design rule and not a bug. Copying a body means copying its LIMBS, so a mimicked shape changes what you can hold and where you can be hurt.

throwing_things.title: Throwing Things
throwing_things.description: Items, weapons and armour can be thrown, up to eight tiles, diagonals included, with a physics simulation driven by the item's weight. Heavy things go a short way and land hard. A thrown item persists where it lands and can be picked up again, by you or by anybody else who finds it.

corpses,_rewards_and_cooldowns.title: Corpses, Rewards and Cooldowns
corpses,_rewards_and_cooldowns.description: After a fight, the reward popup names everything gained at once: items in their rarity colours, money, experience and knowledge. The creature you killed leaves a corpse on the map. Enemy events are removed or locked with a cooldown rather than instantly respawning, so a cleared area stays cleared for a while. Knowledge from a fight is scaled by the enemies' levels against your party's median, so farming things far beneath you is worth almost nothing. Every creature you meet is written into the Bestiary, which belongs to the world rather than to your savegame: a second playthrough adds to the same book instead of starting it again.

elements_how_they_work.title: Elements: How They Work
elements_how_they_work.description: There are nine damage types: Physical, Fire, Ice, Thunder, Water, Petro, Wind, Sacred and Cursed. Every creature answers to each of them with a rate. Above 100% is a weakness, below is a resistance, 0% is immunity, and a negative rate means it ABSORBS that element and is healed by it. The battle HUD prints what you have discovered about the enemy in front of you, so weaknesses are learned by fighting rather than by reading a table. The Bestiary keeps what you learned. States interact with elements directly. Wet raises the damage lightning does; Oily invites fire; Static absorbs lightning and doubles down on water. Setting up an element is often worth more than a bigger attack. A class leans toward an element, and a weapon or a modifier can carry one.

element_physical.title: Element: Physical
element_physical.description: Plain force: edges, points, weight and fists. It is what most weapons do and what most armour is built to stop. Physical damage is the one element that interacts with the body part system most directly, because it is what severs limbs, breaks guards and lands the holds. Heavy armour resists it and encourages Intimidation; light armour trades that away for Stealth. Things without a body in the ordinary sense, spirits, oozes, gases, tend to shrug it off.

element_fire.title: Element: Fire
element_fire.description: Burning. It applies Burned, which keeps hurting after the blow that caused it, and it is answered enormously by anything oily, dry or made of wood. Fire is resisted by the wet and the cold blooded, and absorbed by things that live in it. Setting an enemy on fire and then leaving it alone is a legitimate plan.

element_ice.title: Element: Ice
element_ice.description: Cold. It applies Cold and, taken far enough, Freeze, which stops a body acting altogether. Ice slows things down: a frozen body is a body that is not taking its turn. Against anything already wet it bites much harder, and against anything burning it is a way of putting the fire out, which is not always what you want.

element_thunder.title: Element: Thunder
element_thunder.description: Lightning. It applies Static and, at strength, Paralysis. Thunder is the element with the sharpest conditional: against a WET target it is devastating, and against something already Static it is absorbed and heals it instead. Read the states on the enemy before choosing it. Machines and constructs are usually made of the wrong stuff to enjoy it.

element_water.title: Element: Water
element_water.description: Water applies Wet, which is the setup element of the whole system: it raises lightning damage, it dampens fire, and several states read it. On its own it is rarely the biggest number on the table. Used first, it makes the next attack the biggest number on the table.

element_petro.title: Element: Petro
element_petro.description: Oil, and everything that comes out of the ground with it. Petro is this world's own element and it does not behave like the classical four. It belongs to the petrodemons, which are not creatures so much as forces: they cannot be talked to, petted, recruited or reasoned with, and what they leave behind is measured in barrels rather than in coins. Oil is a currency in this game as well as a substance: it prices the post between worlds, it holds the petrodemon summon on the field, and the market trades it. Petro damage is greasy, choking and industrial. It leaves things flammable.

element_wind.title: Element: Wind
element_wind.description: Air, pressure and cutting motion. Wind is the mobility element: it unbalances, it moves things, and it is what flying creatures both deal and resist. Against anything airborne it is the reliable answer, and against anything rooted or heavy it is the least useful thing you could have brought.

element_sacred.title: Element: Sacred
element_sacred.description: The consecrated element. It is answered terribly by the undead and by the cursed, and it is the one damage type that also heals what it is aimed at when that thing is on the right side of the line. Sacred workings tend to carry protection and purging alongside their damage, so a sacred build is usually also a support build. Several of them sit deep in schools that charge a great deal of knowledge.

element_cursed.title: Element: Cursed
element_cursed.description: The opposite pole: rot, ruin, draining and the debt magic takes out on the caster. It is what the undead deal and what the sacred answers. Cursed workings often cost something beyond MP, and the strongest of them are tagged Forbidden, which puts them alone in the heart of their school's circle and prices them at a hundred times their worth. Used against the living it is among the most efficient damage in the game. Used against something already dead it is a favour.

the_world_map.title: The World Map
the_world_map.description: The world map is one map of Europe, and every tile on it is a whole region. Walking one tile there costs ten minutes of game time, two in a vehicle. M cycles the map display: hidden, minimap in the corner, fullscreen. In fullscreen, drag to pan, wheel or Q and E to zoom. Place names are drawn over the settlements they belong to. Stepping onto a tile does not drop you into it. A travel decision appears: you can keep going, or visit that square, which builds the local map for it. T switches between the world map and the local map you were last in. Loose party members keep a hard leash of two tiles up there, because one tile is a region of the continent and a companion who wandered seven of them has walked into another country. Some squares carry a "???" marker. Those are adventures, and they have their own page.

procedural_maps.title: Procedural Maps
procedural_maps.description: Almost everywhere you walk is generated rather than drawn by hand. A world map square becomes a real map the moment you enter it, built from the world seed and that square's own coordinates, which means it is the SAME map every time you go back, and the same map for every savegame of that world. What goes into one: - The biome of the square, which decides the tileset and everything that grows on it. - Roads, laid as straight runs, crossroads, T junctions and corners, with centre lines painted on them. A road that leads nowhere loops back at the centre of the map rather than running off the edge. - Rivers, wide and irregular, whose banks wander freely but SNAP to a fixed width where they cross a map border, so the river continues correctly into the next square. A river only reaches a border when the square beyond is water too. - Coastlines and beaches, sampled from the world seed along the border line they sit on, so two neighbouring squares draw one continuous shore. - Prefabs: hand authored 32x32 pieces dropped into the square, avoiding the roads. - Terrain features, single tiles and multi tile pieces, scattered by biome. Walking off the edge of a procedural map takes you to the neighbouring square's map, seamlessly, without going back to the world map.

biomes.title: Biomes
biomes.description: The biome of a square decides its tileset, its terrain features, its fauna, its music, its weather and what you can forage there. A handful of biomes are SPECIAL variants, rolled rather than fixed: spirit woods, crystal fields. Certain creatures live in one of those and nowhere else, and a special biome map always places at least one of them, whatever the spawn mode and whatever the calendar has done to the level bands.
