Roofed biomes exist too: cellars, temple interiors, cave dens, dungeons. Those are entered through a structure entrance rather than walked into. Biome names are printed through one service, so a biome reads the same everywhere in the game.

structures_under_the_map.title: Structures Under the Map
structures_under_the_map.description: Procedural maps carry entrances, and an entrance is WALKED INTO rather than pressed. Stepping onto a grate opens it; walking into a cave mouth or a staircase against a wall opens that. What is behind it is ROLLED per entrance tile, seeded on the world seed, the world square and the tile, so one stairway always leads to the same place, and two stairways on the same square rarely lead to the same kind of place. - Stairs down: any structure at all. Cellar, dungeon, crypt, catacombs, mine, cistern, warren, oubliette, library, forge, bunker, laboratory, shrine, tunnel, grotto, lava tube, barrow, station, salt works, cave den, temple. - Stairs up: the things built above ground and buried since. Temples, shrines, libraries, barrows. - A cave: the cave family. Dens, frozen caves, crystal caves, fungal caves, lava tubes, sea grottoes. - A grate: a sewer, and only a sewer. They belong to the towns that declare one underneath them. - A hatch: a patron's vault, which is a cellar written large, buried in gold and rare weapons. Which structures a square can offer depends on what is on the surface: ice fields keep frozen caves under them, a graveyard keeps catacombs.

houses,_inns_and_shops.title: Houses, Inns and Shops
houses,_inns_and_shops.description: Doors on a procedural map are handed to the building system, which owns the interiors. There are pools of houses, inns, shops and tower blocks, and which one is behind a given door is seeded by its coordinates, so a door is always the same business. Buildings can be multi floor and are configured as data rather than drawn one at a time. A shop or an inn wears its name over the door. Doors open with an animation when you walk into them, and the lock is checked BEFORE the animation runs, so a locked door does not tease you.

working_the_terrain.title: Working the Terrain
working_the_terrain.description: On a procedural map, pressing the action button while facing a terrain feature offers to do something with it: - Trees: fell them. Needs an axe in the inventory. - Rocks: mine them. Needs a war pick, any heavy weapon, or a chipped pickaxe. - Plants: pick them up. Needs nothing. - Anything at all: dismantle it. You are paid in crafting materials, the same ones the workbench and the furniture builder use. Mining sometimes turns up an ingot. FORAGING is the interesting one. Picking foliage, herbs and mushrooms always pays plant matter and, roughly two picks in five, a real edible on top of it. What turns up depends on the COUNTRY you are standing in: acorns and chanterelles in a forest, cloudberries on the tundra, dates and prickly pear in a desert, cattail root and samphire on a marsh, blind mushrooms underground. The draw is weighted, so a common berry turns up constantly and a rare one hardly ever, and training Foraging raises the odds. A few features are a specific plant, wheat, corn, sunflower, cactus, kelp, reed, mushroom, and pay that plant whatever the country. Alien surfaces forage nothing. Another world's flora is not a hedgerow, and what it offers is butchered off the local wildlife instead. Everything you remove is remembered in the world folder, keyed by world square, so a tree felled in one savegame stays felled for every savegame of that world, and it is not put back when the map is generated again. That includes scenery inside a prefab: the tree you cut down in a prefab orchard is stamped bare every time that square is rebuilt, but the same prefab standing somewhere else still has all its trees.

the_dungeon_and_the_tower.title: The Dungeon and the Tower
the_dungeon_and_the_tower.description: There is one great dungeon, and its layout belongs to the world: it is rolled when the world is created, so every savegame of that world descends through the same hundred floors. Above ground it runs in ten levels, A through J, each of nine ordinary floors and one elevator floor. The elevator and the floor list let you jump to any floor you have already reached; floors you have not seen show as question marks. Below ground is the LOWER TOWER, ninety two generated floors down. Each of them is one of the structures from the procedural catalogue, rolled from the world seed. The staircases read the other way round down there: deeper is a SMALLER number, so going down takes you from -21 to -22. Every floor is checked for a valid staircase before it is used, so a generated dungeon cannot strand you.

puzzles.title: Puzzles
puzzles.description: Maps carry real puzzles rather than switch hunts. What you will run into: - Sokoban pushing: blocks that slide, pits that swallow them, goal tiles, reset shrines and an undo shrine when you have wedged yourself. - Pressure plates, timed plates that must be held, levers and gates wired with AND and OR logic. - Ice floors you slide across, arrow tiles that shove you, conveyors. - Crystal switches that flip whole sets of blocks between solid and open. - Torches to light, sometimes with a timer and sometimes spreading fire between them. - Colour tiles and lights out grids. - Coloured doors needing a key item, and combination locks. - Warp pads, crackable walls, timed tiles, light beams to redirect, clones that copy your every move, magnetic objects, counterweights and rooms you flood with water.

fog_of_war.title: Fog of War
fog_of_war.description: Some maps are covered by fog you push back by walking through it, with a vision CONE rather than a circle: you see where you are facing, and turning around is how you look about. What you have uncovered is remembered per map, so a place you have explored stays explored.

digging_and_secret_doors.title: Digging and Secret Doors
digging_and_secret_doors.description: Some walls can be broken through at runtime, which turns a dead end into a route. Digging is the deliberate version of that. Secret doors look like wall until you interact with them. Then they fade, make a noise, and stay open. Some doors are not secret at all, only locked. There you have three options: peek through first, pick the lock, or break in. Peeking teleports you for a look without letting you move, and the menu that follows is where the other two live. Picking a lock plays a falling block minigame and needs lockpicks. Breaking in is a crime and will be filed as one.

water,_climbing_and_bridges.title: Water, Climbing and Bridges
water,_climbing_and_bridges.description: Facing water and pressing the action button opens a menu of what you can do with it. Clicking an adjacent water tile does the same. - SWIM. Your sprite changes, your companions are hidden, and you cannot sprint while swimming. - FISH, if the party is carrying a rod. It pays random items, and sometimes an encounter instead. - DIVE, which is how you get under the surface. Terrain marked as climbable can be CLIMBED, slowly, facing upward, with your companions hidden and event interaction suppressed so nothing triggers by accident. Height is tracked while you climb, and jumping down costs 5% of your health per tile fallen, from three tiles up. Jumping north is an ordinary jump. Bridges are layered. Step onto a bridge from its approach and you walk ON it; step on from anywhere else and you pass UNDER it. The state follows you across the whole span and your companions stay on the same layer you do. Standing in front of a mirror shows an upright reflection of whoever is there, and events north of water are reflected in it.

weather,_time_and_seasons.title: Weather, Time and Seasons
weather,_time_and_seasons.description: The clock runs from 8 AM on the 1st of January 2001 and never stops. Time advances as you walk, and jumps when you sleep, wait, or travel. Weather is generated per country, seeded on the real date, and changes when you enter an outdoor map. The current country decides sunrise and sunset, the seasonal day and night temperatures, and what weather is plausible. Weather has teeth: - Rain makes you Wet, which is a state with real consequences in combat. - A storm makes you Static. - Snow makes you Hot, which sounds wrong and is: the body burning to stay warm. The screen is tinted by the time of day and by the temperature, blue for cold and red for hot. Indoors you keep the temperature tint and lose the time of day one. Rain and night bring their own ambient sound, on their own audio channel so they layer over the map's music rather than replacing it.

dreams.title: Dreams
dreams.description: Sleeping sometimes drops you into a dream, and a dream is a place rather than a cutscene. It is a full 3D world rolled from a seed, in the manner of Yume Nikki, LSD Dream Emulator and Blame!. A dream deals four to seven REGIONS and mixes them: backrooms, offices, escher stairs, drowned places, miniatures, cosmic voids, megastructures, car parks, hospitals, cathedrals, factories, datacentres, carnivals, sewers, tundra, desert, fleshpits, gardens and ruins. A backrooms corridor opens onto a drowned car park with a kilometre high structure going up behind it. In there: - WASD walks, the mouse looks, space jumps, and holding jump standing still takes off into flight. - The action button uses whatever weapon is in your right hand, and the d-pad or wheel changes it, stepping a shuffled rack of every weapon in the game. - TOUCHING anything alive strobes and drops you into another dream. - WALKING INTO A WALL, head on, for a moment or in several shoves, does the same. A wall is a link. - Some regions are DRIFT regions: stand in one and the world changes around you. - HOLES have nothing under them. Fall far enough and you leave the dream the fast way. Every dream carries one to three LAWS that are what makes it unlike the last: the ground breathes, gravity is light or crushing, the colours invert, the figures only move while unwatched, or they all come at once, or time hitches, or nothing ever speaks alone, or you are never the same size twice, or the water rises and lets go again, or the dream repeats itself repeats itself. The dream never ends: the ground loops in every direction and is stacked in decks going up for as long as anybody climbs. Every minute in there rolls a chance of KNOWLEDGE, and what you carried out is reported when you wake. Escape opens the wake up prompt: pinch your cheeks to wake, or keep dreaming.

adventures_on_the_map.title: Adventures on the Map
adventures_on_the_map.description: A handful of world map squares carry a "???" marker, redrawn once a day. Standing on one, or facing it from next door, and choosing Investigate plays a branching adventure written for that place. It is a real choose your own path encounter: every choice leads somewhere and the last node pays out. A relic, gear, salvage, money, a fight with something native, a minigame, an augment, a change in your standing with a faction, a crime filed against you, a rest that puts real percentage points back into everybody's needs, or the walk back with nothing. The party LEADER is the one who goes down there, and the companion at their shoulder comments on what is happening in their own register, so a Cautious companion and a Cynical one narrate the same scene differently. Some choices are only offered to a leader of a particular temperament. The prose is combinatorial, so the same adventure never reads the same way twice, and it names the actual people who walked out there. A biome carries one marker, or two if it is very large, and a named place, a country or a hyperpower's territory carries its own on top of that. A square you have answered is answered for good. Everything you did is written into the diary.

bologna.title: Bologna
bologna.description: One real city is in the game as itself: Bologna, rasterised from OpenStreetMap into a grid of large cells that join seamlessly at their borders. Every building the importer rasterised has a door on its south face, and every one of those doors is a way in. Most are homes; a share are shops and inns, seeded per cell and per tile, so a given door is always the same business, and it wears its name over it. The cells carry no hand placed events at all, so the city is populated at runtime: a crowd of townspeople drawn from a mix of the world's own faces and Bolognesi born in the city, plus wildlife placed by habitat, street animals on the pavement, park animals on the green, waterfowl and fish in the canals, birds on the rooftops.

platformer_maps.title: Platformer Maps
platformer_maps.description: Some maps are not top down at all. On a map tagged as a platform stage, the controls become a side scroller: left and right walk, space jumps, shift runs, gravity pulls, and pressing jump against a wall wall jumps off it. Ladders are climbed by pressing up. Your companions follow the exact path you took, a moment behind, facing the way you faced.

flying.title: Flying
flying.description: When something grants flight, you move like an airship: freely, in any direction, over everything. Pressing confirm lands you again. Flight is granted by particular items, skills and vehicles rather than being a standing ability, and landing puts you back under the ordinary rules of the terrain you came down on.

the_map_of_maps.title: The Map of Maps
the_map_of_maps.description: There is a second kind of map: a graph of every map you know and how they connect, built from the transfer events and doors between them. Click a node to make it your destination and the shortest path from where you are is highlighted. A compass then appears in the corner of the screen pointing at the next waypoint on that path, and it disappears when you arrive or when you deselect the destination. The choice survives closing the map. It is the practical answer to "how do I get back to that place I found".

chests_and_treasure_rooms.title: Chests and Treasure Rooms
chests_and_treasure_rooms.description: Chests belong to the world rather than to your savegame, so one emptied by one playthrough is empty for the rest, and which chests stand open is remembered. What is in them is generated against the party's median level. Some maps hide TREASURE ROOMS: reachable, randomly placed rooms whose contents justify the search. They are worth the wall you had to dig through.

research_and_discovery.title: Research and Discovery
research_and_discovery.description: Seven trees of discovery, one per discipline: Social Sciences, Alchemistry, Technomagica, Physics, Arcane, Mathematics, Astronomy and Theotecnical. The scientific trees follow the real arc of progress from 2001 to 2012. The Arcane and Technomagica trees follow the in world rediscovery of lost magic and its fusion with machinery, and the Theotecnical tree follows the Vatican rebuilding its dogma around engines. Each also carries fringe pseudoscientific side branches and a handful of nodes generated from your world's own seed. A DISCOVERY BELONGS TO THE WORLD. Completed nodes, and the name of the party leader who got there first, live in the world folder, so every savegame of that world shares the same tech tree. The permanent bonuses are applied to every party in the world; the one off rewards go only to the party that discovered it. Researching a node consumes crafting materials and hands most of that cost back as refined byproducts, so research feeds the crafting economy instead of draining it.

fast_travel.title: Fast Travel
fast_travel.description: Any place marked as a destination can be travelled to rather than walked to. Bus stops and signposts on the roads are the visible half of this; the travel screen is the rest. Choosing a destination and a mode does not cut to the arrival. You are put on a TRAVEL MAP for that kind of transport, the train, the coach, the taxi, and a countdown runs while you are aboard. That timer is persistent: it keeps running while you open menus, fight, or do anything else, and it survives changing scenes. When it reaches zero you get out at the other end. Which means travel is time you can use. Your companions talk to each other in transit, the crew of a vehicle sleeps in shifts, and the clock outside keeps moving: the world ages while you are on the road.

the_thirty_ways_to_travel.title: The Thirty Ways to Travel
the_thirty_ways_to_travel.description: Every destination lists the transports that actually reach it. There are thirty, and they trade money against time. Free, or nearly: - Walking. Costs nothing, takes the longest. - Bicycle. Cheap and slightly quicker. - Car sharing and the camper. These cost no MONEY at all: they burn fuel instead. - Horse. Cheap, and better than a bicycle. Public and ordinary: - Bus, train, taxi, boat, ferry. The train is fast for its price; the taxi is the same speed for twice as much. Expensive: - Economy flight, business flight, limousine, helicopter, private jet. A private jet is ten times as fast as walking, and priced accordingly. - Cruise and submarine. Slow, and a submarine is one of the dearest things on the board. - Balloon and zeppelin. Slow, expensive, and worth doing once. Exotic: - Magic carpet and dragon. Very fast, very expensive. - Teleport circle. Twenty times walking speed for a modest fee, when you can find one. - Hypermetro, maglev, hyperloop. The infrastructure of a world that has other physics. - Starship, wormhole, quantum, time machine, dimensional. These are not transport in the ordinary sense and they are priced like it: a dimensional crossing costs a thousand times the base fare and is a thousand times as fast. Cost is the base fare multiplied by distance; speed divides the time. Pick the line you can afford.

owning_a_vehicle.title: Owning a Vehicle
owning_a_vehicle.description: A vehicle is proven by an ITEM. Holding the key, the deed or the broom is what makes that vehicle appear in the Vehicles menu, and what makes it summonable and drivable. Vehicles are parked in the world, not carried in your pocket. Where each one stands is remembered, including which world square and which underground layer, so a camper left in one biome does not turn up standing in the next one. If several vehicles are parked on one tile only the last is drawn, and interacting asks which one you meant. Walking up to a parked vehicle and interacting opens its menu: start driving, enter the interior, use its storage, refuel, repair. Three of them, the camper, the car and the starship, have real INTERIORS: maps you walk around inside, with storage holds that are the practical answer to carrying capacity.

vehicle_the_camper.title: Vehicle: The Camper
vehicle_the_camper.description: The big one, and the closest thing to a home you own. It carries a hundred litres of fuel, has a walk in interior with beds and storage, can be repaired and upgraded, and refuels at any roadside pump. It is a ground vehicle, so it crosses road tiles on the world map faster than open country. Fast travel by camper costs no money at all, only fuel. With the workshop upgrades fitted it stops being only a road vehicle: the AQUATIC module lets it float and dive, and the FLIGHT module gives it rotors. F takes off and lands, C dives and surfaces over water, and driving onto water simply floats it. Driving it is a full 3D scene of its own. See the driving page. A crew lives aboard it: somebody holds the wheel and the others sleep in the back, in shifts. See the crew page.

vehicle_the_car.title: Vehicle: The Car
vehicle_the_car.description: Faster than the camper and much smaller. Sixty litres of fuel, its own small interior, repairable and upgradable, and it refuels at any pump. Like the camper it takes the road bonus on the world map, and fast travel by car costs fuel rather than money. A car is also the one vehicle you can acquire by crime. Any parked car on the map can be stolen: face it, press the action button, and choose to steal it. That opens the lockpicking minigame and requires a lockpick, or a skeleton key, which opens it outright. Succeed and you gain its keys and the car leaves the world; fail and a vehicle theft is filed against you, and the lockpick is gone.

vehicle_the_bike.title: Vehicle: The Bike
vehicle_the_bike.description: Human powered, so it never needs fuel and can never run out. It is the fastest thing you can own early, it takes the road bonus, and it has no interior, no storage and no repairs to pay for. There is no crew rota on a bike. The rider pedals it and that is the whole arrangement: nobody naps in the back of a bicycle.

vehicle_the_flying_broom.title: Vehicle: The Flying Broom
vehicle_the_flying_broom.description: The bike with the ground taken away. It needs no fuel, it is welcome INDOORS, and it stows back into your pack as an item. What sets it apart is that it FLIES. A flying vehicle passes over every tile of every map: walls, water, cliffs and events alike. And it lands on anything you could conceivably stand on, including rooftops, cliff tops and bridges, which no other vehicle can reach. It sets down where it hovers and is boarded again from the tile it landed on. A road is no shortcut to something that never touches one, so the broom takes no road bonus. It does not need one.

vehicle_the_boat.title: Vehicle: The Boat
vehicle_the_boat.description: An inflatable dinghy. No fuel, no interior, no storage and no repairs, and it travels only on open water. The party is drawn ABOARD it rather than vanishing into a hull: everybody sits on the benches, bow first, so the party always faces the way it is travelling, and the pet sits in the stern.

vehicle_the_starship.title: Vehicle: The Starship
vehicle_the_starship.description: The ship that leaves the planet. Two hundred litres of fuel, a full walk in interior, and it CANNOT be refuelled at a roadside pump: this is not a thing you top up on the way to the shops. It is generated rather than drawn: the hull, the layout and the look are built procedurally from a set of trait axes and can be edited, so your ship is your ship and nobody else's. The starship needs no driver. It flies itself, which is why the crew page is about how people LIVE aboard it rather than who is holding the wheel. It is what the star map is for. See the Galaxy pages.

fuel.title: Fuel
fuel.description: The camper, the car and the starship burn fuel; the bike, the broom and the boat never do. Fuel is bought at pumps, and the price moves with the world's own oil market rather than being a fixed number: a refuel is a small trade. The camper and the car can fill up at any roadside pump, the starship cannot. Fuel is consumed by distance travelled, at a rate that differs per vehicle, and a fuel gauge sits in the corner of the screen while you are driving one. Running dry strands you where you stand. Fast travel by camper or car spends fuel INSTEAD of money, which is what makes owning one worth the maintenance.

vehicle_damage_and_repair.title: Vehicle Damage and Repair
vehicle_damage_and_repair.description: A vehicle is not one condition bar. It has twelve parts, each with its own health: engine, transmission, brakes and steering, which are CRITICAL and stop the vehicle dead when they break, plus battery, alternator, radiator, fuel system, exhaust, suspension, tyres and body, which only degrade its performance. Damage is real and comes from what you actually do. Hitting something soft marks the front of the vehicle only; hitting another vehicle at road speed is felt all through it. The parts damaged are named in the notification. Repairs consume crafting materials, scaled by how deep the repair is, so keeping a vehicle on the road is part of the crafting economy. The condition of the whole vehicle is drawn as an HP bar on the party HUD while you are riding it, with its fuel where a person's magic would be.

the_workshop.title: The Workshop
the_workshop.description: Vehicles are upgraded with crafting materials at the workshop. Four upgrades have three levels each: - Acceleration - Speed - Fuel capacity, which the bike and the boat have no use for - Structural health And two are one off modules, for the camper only: - AQUATIC: it floats and it dives. - FLIGHT: rotors, take off and land. There is also aerodynamic work that reduces how much game time a tile of the world map costs you, which on a long crossing is worth more than raw speed. Each level costs progressively more exotic materials, from steel and plastic up through titanium and circuitry to varlenian matter, nanotubes and quantum components.

the_crew.title: The Crew
the_crew.description: A journey is four people shut in a cabin, one of them holding the wheel. The leader takes the wheel when a journey starts and the HUD says so. Only the DRIVER earns the vehicle's specialization experience: the three people asleep in the back are not learning to sail. Time at the wheel is tracked per person as STRAIN, and alertness is the party's sleep meter less that member's own strain. When the driver's alertness drops under 40%, the wheel changes hands to the best rested member above that line, and everyone not driving sheds strain, so a crew of three takes turns across a long haul. When nobody is fit to relieve the driver, they keep going and you are told so: stopping is your call. Everyone not driving actually SLEEPS. Naps start only under 40% sleep, and then run to full or to the end of the journey. Sleepers carry the Sleep state, so the HUD shows it. They are woken when the nap ends, when the party gets out, when somebody steps into the cabin, and by a CRASH, which also keeps them awake for the next hour. The bike and the broom have no rota: their rider does everything. The starship has no driver at all, and there the crew instead tends one need at a time, a meal, a wash, a conversation, a game, a shift of sleep, changing their minds halfway through as often as not. Eating aboard consumes real food out of the hold, and with an empty hold they go and do something else.

driving_in_3d.title: Driving in 3D
driving_in_3d.description: Driving the camper opens a full 3D road scene built out of the world map itself: the same grid of biomes, with mountains as noise height fields, water as flat blue, roads as dual lane asphalt running the way the road tiles run, and everything else as ground in that biome's own colour, blended smoothly at the seams. Coastlines slope into the sea, and cities, forests and cacti are scattered along the way. Three views, swapped with Tab or the pad's Y button: - FIRST PERSON DRIVING, at the wheel, behind an animated steering wheel and a working dash. - CAR, a chase camera. The same controls, with zoom on the wheel or the triggers. - CABIN, a free roam view inside the vehicle, reached by interacting with a door. W throttles, Shift is the turbo, S brakes and reverses, A and D steer, space is the handbrake, and the mouse looks around. The driving model is a real one: a five speed automatic gearbox with an RPM engine note, lateral slip so the handbrake drifts, surface grip that differs between asphalt, dirt, grass, sand, snow and rock, gravity on slopes, and a chassis that follows the terrain. The traffic is real too: nine vehicle models, hatchback, saloon, coupe, SUV, pickup, taxi, panel van, box truck and city bus, built at true size against the camper, with glass you can see through and wheels that visibly roll and steer. They brake, they take junctions properly, and they can be crashed into. A bus shoves harder than a hatchback. On foot out there the leader's own weapon is in frame and in hand: click or press the shoulder buttons to swing it, and the d-pad steps through every weapon in the party's bags that the leader can hold, really changing their equipment. Enemies matched to the biome idle by the roadside, so a drive is not empty.

traffic,_roadkill_and_theft.title: Traffic, Roadkill and Theft
traffic,_roadkill_and_theft.description: The cars driving around the map are driven by the game rather than by event pages, which is why they behave like traffic instead of like scenery. A car is as big as its SPRITE, not as its tile: a car drawn three tiles long occupies three tiles for every purpose, so it never clips a wall it drives past, cars collide bodywork against bodywork, and anybody standing under the bodywork is run over. Only a car that is MOVING hits anything. A parked car is solid and harmless. Town traffic brakes for people; highway traffic does not. Being hit knocks you clear and triggers an accident. An NPC hit by a car is really injured: injury conditions are written onto their profile and show up on their health tab afterwards. A creature hit hard enough dies outright and leaves a harvestable corpse. Driving over somebody YOURSELF is different again. Running down an NPC injures them, drops their opinion of every party member, and files a hit and run against you. Running down a creature flings it off the bonnet the first two times; from the third, the odds it turns and fights you climb steeply, and about five rams kill it, so a persistent rammer usually gets a fight rather than a corpse. And the car feels it: the parts damaged are named. Now and then a car pulls over and its driver GETS OUT, walks about, talks to people, and eventually drives on. That driver is a real person with the ordinary wandering behaviour. The car sits there parked and stealable the whole time, which is rather the point.

people_are_real_here.title: People Are Real Here
people_are_real_here.description: Nobody on the map is scenery with a line of dialogue attached. Every person carries a full profile, generated deterministically from their name and the world seed, which means the same person is the same person in every savegame of that world: - a personality out of twenty five archetypes, which decides how they speak - traits, exactly like the ones your characters carry - an ideology on five axes: economy, authority, tradition, militarism, mysticism - wealth, skills, an inventory and equipment - a faction, a home, a job and a working schedule - a backstory drawn from the actual history of your world: the events they lived through, where they were born and in what year - a medical history, including diseases they have had and bones that healed badly A share of the population is not people at all. The stray dog on the corner, the thing in the cellar: creatures are minted from the same system, and a creature on a beast class is genuinely non sentient. It holds no conversation, takes no political side, never saves toward a better house, never moves, and starts with no money.

the_empathize_panel.title: The Empathize Panel
the_empathize_panel.description: Talking to somebody properly opens the Empathize panel, which is that person's whole sheet: who they are, their history, their biology, their health, their romantic life, their day to day life, their politics, and a log of the last conversations they had with other people. From it you can talk, praise, insult, joke, give, trade, court, propose, recruit, and read exactly why they feel the way they do about you. Crucially, standings here are PER PARTY MEMBER. An NPC does not have an opinion of "the party": they have an opinion of each of your characters, and it is the member doing the talking whose standing moves. The panel shows every member's standing so you can send the right person to do the talking. There is also a free chat: you can type, and the answer is generated. If a local language model has been enabled in the experimental options, it writes the reply; otherwise a Markov chain does.

how_somebody_decides_what_they_think_of_.title: How Somebody Decides What They Think of You
how_somebody_decides_what_they_think_of_.description: What an NPC actually thinks of one of your characters is built out of four things, and only the first is earned by talking: - The BASE opinion, moved by everything you have ever done to them: kindness, insults, gifts, trades, crimes they know about. - TRAIT COMPATIBILITY. Some traits get on and some do not, and this is applied before a word is said. - IDEOLOGY. How close your creeds stand on the five axes, worth up to a dozen points either way. - HYGIENE. How the two of you smell to each other, right now. This is the only part of the number that changes with a bath, and it is explained in full on its own page under Needs. Gaining standing with somebody also feeds the social need of the character who gained it, so being liked is worth something mechanically. ATTRACTION is tracked separately from opinion, because liking somebody and wanting them are not the same number. Ordinary conversation, gifts and trade move opinion alone; only courting moves attraction. It starts at zero and is earned, and how likely a romantic move is to land reads trait compatibility and hygiene a second time, at their own heavier weight.

people_have_lives.title: People Have Lives
people_have_lives.description: Every person in the world lives their life whether or not you are watching, and it advances whenever time does: minute by minute, and through any time skip, sleeping, waiting or travelling. - They were born somewhere, on a date, and they have a record of every move they have made since and why. - They meet, date, marry, divorce and abandon each other, preferring partners from their own settlement. - They have careers built from the real job list, with a job history from their first working year to today, changes as they age, and retirement in old age. - Honest ones keep clean records. Dishonest ones carry criminal histories: past convictions, sentences served or still being served off screen in prison, outstanding bounties, and a standing that all of it drags down and that slowly recovers once the debts are paid. - A conviction can cost somebody their job. None of this is scripted. It is sampled forward at the rate life happens, so a year spent in cryogenic sleep is a year in which everybody you know got older, changed jobs, married and buried each other.

what_people_say_to_each_other.title: What People Say to Each Other
what_people_say_to_each_other.description: Two people who wander close together can stop, face each other and hold a real conversation, played out one line at a time in thought bubbles over their heads. The tone of it, positive, negative, neutral or a debate, comes from what they think of each other and from their two personalities. Finishing a conversation moves both of their opinions and is recorded as "met so and so". People sharing a room while busy trade quick two line exchanges without stopping what they are doing. Every one of the twenty five personalities has its own voice: its own lines for the weather and the time of day, its own inner monologue, and its own openers and closers that colour any shared line it delivers, so two people saying "the same" thing do not sound alike. The last twenty conversations of every person are kept in the world folder and can be read in their panel, so you can find out what people have been saying about you.

settlements_and_what_happens_to_them.title: Settlements and What Happens To Them
settlements_and_what_happens_to_them.description: Every settlement carries three civic meters that every other system can feel: - PROSPERITY, from employment, the national economy and recent events. - SECURITY, from real crime per head, the honesty of the local captain of the guard (a crooked captain rots a town), national stability, and how wanted YOU are. - MOOD, built from the other two plus national unrest, festivals, epidemics and how busy the streets are. On top of the meters sit EPISODES, which turn slow drift into events with a shape: - A CRIME WAVE starts when security collapses. While it runs, crime is more tempting and the crackdown catches more thieves, so the wave breaks itself. - BOOMS and BUSTS start at the extremes of prosperity and swing hiring, crime, divorce, shop prices and market sentiment, then erode their own cause. - A FESTIVAL is declared by a thriving town: mood and bustle up, shops fuller, and pickpockets working the crowds. - An EPIDEMIC is rare and worse in miserable towns: mood, hiring and shop traffic collapse and hygiene drains fast until it burns out. Every transition feeds back out: into the news, into the stock market, into how often people are hired or commit crimes, into how hard it is to steal, into national politics, and into what people gossip about. Unemployment feeds crime, crime feeds crackdowns, crackdowns feed prisons, prisons feed unemployment. It is circular on purpose.

politics.title: Politics
politics.description: Every hyperpower has a real government, and its shape differs: theocracies, single party states, parliamentary monarchies, technocracies, sultanates, divine pantheons, serene republics, corporatocracies, warband confederacies. Each has parties or orders or clans, a political class with charisma, integrity, cunning and ambition, a head of state, and running meters of legitimacy, stability, unrest, economy and treasury. Elections happen in each power's own idiom: parliamentary general elections, papal conclaves with several ballots, politburo plenums announcing 99% results, wealth weighted shareholder meetings, goblin moots where the runner up risks being eaten, divine ascension tournaments, palace successions, and the Archive's Great Examination. Every result is recorded permanently. Between elections there are scandals, edicts, protests, riots, coups, revolutions, assassinations, referendums, festivals, rumours that spread through the population, and rulers who age and die. Every person has a political identity: their five axis ideology, a party, an engagement level from apathetic through voter and activist to organizer, a voting record, and grudges against the parties that beat theirs. Locally, each settlement elects a MAYOR from its own real population every year, and the mayor appoints a captain of the guard, a tax collector and a high priest from among their ideological allies. Who they pick is felt: that is where the crooked captain who rots a town comes from.

factions_and_reputation.title: Factions and Reputation
factions_and_reputation.description: There are eighteen factions and your standing with each runs from -100 to +100. Reputation is moved by what you do: contracts taken, crimes committed, adventures resolved, sides taken. Factions answer to hyperpowers. A faction with a parent power is a branch of it, which matters when standing moves: earning credit with a parent can carry its branches with it. Standing decides what is offered to you, what prices you are quoted, who will speak to you and who will not, and which seats you may take.

the_assembly.title: The Assembly
the_assembly.description: Every parent power keeps a seat on neutral ground inside the Omega Tower, and once a game week the delegations argue about alliances, trade, war and whatever fell out of the sky that month. A party member can take one of those seats. Nothing happens to the party as a whole: the seat is that character's, the standing it earns is theirs, and the weekly stipend is paid to them, on their standing with the power they serve. A member whose standing falls far enough is dismissed. Only powers that already think neutrally or well of that character will have them. Joining raises their standing with the power and with every branch under it. A character joins once; resigning costs a great deal more than joining paid. A SESSION rolls one to three motions. Two to five delegations take the floor, each in its own voice, you answer, and then EVERY seat votes whether it spoke or not. The ballot is public or secret: public turns each named tile green or red as it is read out, secret shuffles them unlabelled and turns them all at once, so only the tally is certain. GRAVE motions, war, admission, territory, artifacts, theonuclear devices and the goblin question, then go to the Security Council: the five strongest powers your century actually left standing, measured on military, economic, population, information and arcane strength. They approve or veto, majority carries, and a tie is broken by the Secretary General. Without one, it fails. One seat only watches: the Tourists hold a chair and no ballot, take the floor when they feel like it, and are offered to nobody.

crime_and_bounty.title: Crime and Bounty
crime_and_bounty.description: Crimes are real records, not a wanted meter. Every crime you commit is filed by name with its own bounty value, and the sum of them is what the world calls your bounty. You can commit them deliberately: theft, breaking and entering, vehicle theft, hit and run, and a long list of others. You can also commit them by accident, which is what running somebody over is. Bounty is felt everywhere. It lowers the security meter of the settlements you are in, it makes people gossip about you, it changes how the guard behaves, and it is what a court will eventually read out. The crime record can be viewed at any time, and it can be dealt with. See the police page.

the_police_portal.title: The Police Portal
the_police_portal.description: The N€police application on the Hypernet is the continental police portal, and it is how a citizen deals with their own record without waiting to be caught. - CASE FILE lists every charge with the fine it carries. Charges can be settled one at a time or all at once, and settling removes them from the record and lowers the bounty. - SELF-REPORT lets you confess something the authorities have not registered. A self filed charge is entered at HALF its usual fine, but it is a real charge: it raises the bounty until it is settled or served. - CUSTODY offers two things: turn yourself in, which puts you straight in a cell where the bounty is ground down by time served, or request a hearing before Eris. Both custody options leave the computer first, because the cells and the courtroom are places.

the_trial.title: The Trial
the_trial.description: Justice in this world is administered by Eris, the ex goddess of discord turned deranged Goddess of Justice, and a trial is a procedural encounter rather than a scripted scene. The courtroom, the gallery, the staff and the ambience are rolled fresh each time, she cites invented case law and produces invented exhibits mid hearing, and every line resolves its alternatives as it is spoken, so no two hearings read alike. THE DEFENCE BAR. Before the hearing opens you retain counsel. There are three options: hire one of five advocates, nominate a party member, or stand alone. The five are real people from your world, fixed for the lifetime of that world and shared by every savegame of it. Their rank is written onto their actual profile, their level, their INT, their WIS, their Law specialization and their job, so they read as lawyers everywhere else in the game too. Recruit one into your party and they are struck off the bar and replaced by the next name in the queue. The brief shows each option's sprite, level, INT, WIS, Law level, how they feel about you, their fee, and the PROJECTED ODDS of every outcome, computed with the same model the verdict actually runs on. Those odds swing hard on the mood Eris turned up in. She greets counsel in her own voice and, depending on that mood, sometimes throws them out of the room, in which case their bonus is gone and the fee is not refunded. LAW IS EARNED BY ARGUING. A defendant who represents themselves, or the companion who stands up instead, gains a few points of the Law specialization per hearing, and their level feeds straight back into the odds. Retaining a professional teaches the party nothing at all. The hearing itself is a plea, guilty or not guilty, and a series of choices. Then a verdict, which is unpredictable and depends heavily on her mood. DATING CHANGES THE LAW. Every evening spent with Eris raises a bond, and a defendant she has had dinner with meets a warmer mood wheel, a lower conviction chance, shorter sentences, and, high enough, an outright dismissal before the charges are even read. She remains fickle: sometimes an evening buys nothing at all, and she will say so. In sandbox mode there is a reverse trial, where you play Eris and judge somebody else.

sentences_and_prison.title: Sentences and Prison
sentences_and_prison.description: A sentence comes in two shapes. - A NAMED TERM is served by the game clock. You go to the cells, time passes, and the bounty is cleared on release. - An OPEN ENDED sentence has no release date and instead grinds the bounty down while you sit in it, day by day, until there is nothing left to serve. Turning yourself in at the police portal takes you straight to the second kind without a hearing, which is sometimes the better deal. Coming out, Eris has something to say about it, and what she says depends on how the two of you stand.

dating_eris.title: Dating Eris
dating_eris.description: Eris can be courted, and an evening with her is a full procedural scene rather than a menu. It happens in a real BIOME, and every biome owns its own opening, its own questions, its own romantic beat, its own chaotic beat, its own shared activity and its own local incidents, so a date on a salt flat reads nothing like a date in a sewer. A scenario is rolled on top of it, picnic, seance, stakeout and others, so the same biome hosts many different evenings. Her MOOD is rolled fresh from sixteen: playful, romantic, chaotic, nervous, confident, caring, guilty, crazed, psyched out, high on solipsism, eldritch, melancholy, smug, paranoid, prophetic, bored. It can shift mid date, changing her voice and her heartbeat. When the mood turns ELDRITCH the thing across the table is not entirely Eris any more: her lines warp, her pulse reads things that are not numbers, and the portrait misbehaves. Each date also rolls a REGISTER, sincere, ordinarily capricious, or completely bonkers, which scales how often the evening is interrupted and how hard her feelings swing. She interrupts with DARES, up to and including robbing a bank. Your own answers are procedural too: any choice list can grow weird, awkward, chaotic or blunt wildcard answers, and how she takes one is a roll of her mood. Two heartbeats are drawn on screen, yours and hers, and both move with every beat of the evening. She REMEMBERS past dates and brings them up. She keeps a separate relationship score for every party member, active or benched, and mid date she sometimes turns on, or towards, one of your companions. The first date that ends well earns a parting gift: a blade seed, once per save. And it feeds directly into the courtroom. See the trial page.

the_post.title: The Post
the_post.description: A world folder is shared by every savegame of that world, and your machine holds several worlds. That is already a postal network: one party can write to another party of the same world, or to a party living in a DIFFERENT world entirely, and the letter waits in their mailbox until somebody plays them. A letter carries a delivery date measured in the recipient world's clock, and the sender may hold it back by days, months or years. Until that date passes, the letter is in transit and does not show. Writing to your own party with a delay is therefore a letter to your future self, and it is offered deliberately. Money and goods can be enclosed. They leave the sender's pockets at once and are handed over once, when the recipient collects them. Inside one world the post is free. Crossing into another world is priced against the two commodities that survive the crossing, oil and souls: their prices multiplied, doubled once per step of dimensional distance between the two worlds, and never less than three hundred thousand euros. In practice that is tens of millions, and between distant dimensions it runs into the billions. It is meant to be ruinous.

the_news.title: The News
the_news.description: The world writes its own news, and the news is not decoration: items carry real effects on property prices and shop occupancy, and other systems read them. Episodes in settlements, riots, coups, elections, epidemics and even the mayor's divorce become headlines. The real estate market moves on them, the stock market takes its sentiment from them, and people talk about them. Reading the news is how you find out what is worth doing this week.

the_party_diary.title: The Party Diary
the_party_diary.description: A diary is not a log. It is the record ONE party kept of its own life, and it outlives that party: a permadeath run whose savegame is deleted leaves its diary standing in the world folder, so a later playthrough of the same world can read what the people before them did. It is written as it happens, and it watches almost everything: journeys and arrivals with the hour, landings on planets, bridge warps, walking into a named place for the first time, going down into a structure, changing dungeon floor, sleeping, waiting, cryogenic sleep and the year it woke in, fights won and what was in them, bosses felled, fleeing, losing, arena streaks, people joining and leaving, deaths, retirements and recalls, levels, pets, creatures talked round, births, pregnancies, friendships and enmities, courtships, evenings with Eris, people you knew dying, diseases caught and recovered from, limbs lost, augments fitted, field surgery, notable finds, artifacts, purchases and sales, thefts, property, loans, share trades, crimes, charges, trials, verdicts, prison, shifts worked, crops sown and reaped, things forged, cooked, brewed and built, skills learned, technologies researched, quests, creatures entered in the bestiary, minigames played, television watched and dreams had. Deliberately NOT watched: ordinary conversation, reading the description of a statue, states coming and going, and throwing things away. It is written as keys rather than as finished prose, so a diary written in one language reads correctly in another. Your companions read it too. The banter system takes the newest lines and turns them into what the party talks about while walking away.

conversation_topics.title: Conversation Topics
conversation_topics.description: Some dialogue teaches you a TOPIC, written in square brackets in the line where it appears. Once one of your characters has heard it, the whole party knows it. Topics are keys to conversations. A dialogue option that requires a topic is not greyed out, it is INVISIBLE until somebody in the party knows the topic, so a conversation you have already had can open doors in a conversation you have not had yet. Every topic learned is announced as it happens, and the Topics tab of this book is the list of them, with who in the party knows each one. Some topics have a page of their own written for them, which appears once you have learned it.

armies.title: Armies
armies.description: Beyond the party of three there is an ARMY, run in the manner of Mount and Blade. Troops are recruited by faction, up to a hundred of them, and their count is drawn over your sprite on the world map. The world map is full of other armies. About a fifth are faction armies of two hundred to a thousand troops, which stay inside their own country's borders and number at least three per country. The rest are independent bands of five to thirty, drawn from several factions, which roam anywhere and spawn near you. They move when you move. Touching one starts a FIELD BATTLE, played out as a real time tactical view in the manner of Total War: your units in yellow, theirs in red, formed up by role, close quarters in front, support behind, ranged at the back, and fighting on their own stats. Wounded troops drop to one hit point and stop fighting; killed troops leave your army for good. The wheel zooms and dragging pans.

multiplayer.title: Multiplayer
multiplayer.description: There are two ways to play with other people. ONLINE, through either a central server or Steam. A server session supports many players, of whom the nearest eight are drawn on any one map, party members first. A Steam lobby is capped at eight. Steam sessions set rich presence, so friends see Join Game in their friends list and can drop in. LOCAL SPLIT SCREEN, with two players on one machine and a gamepad each. The two viewports are independent and MERGE into one when the players are close together. Player two is a full participant: they interact with events and trigger things themselves. Split screen also runs a HOT SEAT for minigames, even without a split screen session on the overworld. Real time arcade carts let either player steer, and turn based games like chess, pool and bowling alternate between the two. During a map battle the two viewports merge for the fight, player two's avatar becomes the second party member's battler, and they drive the command menu on their own character's turn.

the_century_behind_you.title: The Century Behind You
the_century_behind_you.description: Before you ever take a step, your world has already lived through a century: a procedural alternate history of Europe from 1900 to 2001. It generates coups, elections, purges and assassinations; wars, sieges, mutinies and conquests; fifty kinds of paranormal anomaly, occult rites and the Squishing itself; scientific expeditions, natural disasters and organised crime; economic shifts and technological breakthroughs. The weighting favours the paranormal and the occult over background noise. That history is not decoration. It decides which hyperpowers exist and how strong they are, which five sit on the Security Council, what epidemics the last century saw, and what the people you meet actually lived through: their backstories are drawn from it. The whole timeline is readable in the Historical Archive, and the Lore tab of this book carries the chronicle of everything that has happened in your world since, newest first.

money.title: Money
money.description: Money is euros. Internally it is counted in gold at a hundred gold to the euro, which is why prices are written with two decimal places: 1212 gold is 12.12 euros. There is no shop currency and no separate token economy except at the arcade, where euros are exchanged for tokens and back at a fixed rate, either at the converter machine in the world or at the Token Exchange on the Hypernet. Your wealth is not one number. The Assets screen adds up cash in hand, money in the bank, property, shares and livestock, less your debts, and calls the result net worth.

shops.title: Shops
shops.description: Shops come in several kinds and they do not all work alike. - A COUNTER shop is the ordinary sort: a grid of goods with categories, sorted by price, with the full detail card of anything you point at. - A DELIVERY order takes one to seven days to arrive depending on price, and up to six things can be on order at once. You collect them later. - A RANDOM DAILY SHOP is seeded by its own coordinates and the world seed, so every merchant has their own permanent character, and their stock is rerolled each in game day. - A VENDING MACHINE stocks itself the same way, from its coordinates: a 4x4 grid of products with codes, three purchases per slot per day, at least one weird item in every machine, and one machine in ten selling nothing but weird items. Nothing about that stock is stored in your save; it is recomputed from where the machine stands. - TEACHING shops sell skills rather than goods, at a discount. Tax is charged on everything that is not a skill, at a rate that moves with the world's own economy and never drops below thirty percent. What is on the shelves belongs to the world, so a shop cleaned out by one savegame is cleaned out for all of them until it restocks at midnight.

stealing.title: Stealing
stealing.description: Anything on a shop's shelves can be stolen. The steal window scans the map for shop events and lists what they hold, with a success percentage against each item computed from your agility, the item's value and its weight: light and cheap is easy, heavy and precious is not. Ordinary shops are scanned across the whole map. A random daily merchant is only scanned when you are within five tiles of them. Getting caught is a crime, filed with your name on it, and the settlement's security meter feels it. During a crime wave the crackdown makes stealing measurably harder, which is the system arguing with you rather than a flat penalty.

banking_and_loans.title: Banking and Loans
banking_and_loans.description: The bank takes deposits, pays interest on your balance, and lends money at interest against a due date. Interest and loan maturity run on the WORLD clock, so they accrue while you are walking, sleeping, travelling or in cryogenic sleep. Come back from a year in a freezer and your loan has been waiting for you. Failing to repay on time is penalised. The Assets screen shows the balance, the outstanding loan and the due date beside everything else you own.

the_stock_market.title: The Stock Market
the_stock_market.description: The market trades the two commodities that mean anything in this world: OIL and SOUL crystals. It is a single page trading terminal where you buy and sell shares directly with money. Prices are a random walk, but not an indifferent one. Market sentiment is tilted by what is actually happening in the world: booms and busts in settlements, news events, the state of the powers. A bust somewhere real is a dip you can read about first. Prices belong to the WORLD, not to your savegame: every playthrough of that world trades against the same market history. The Assets screen draws the live oil and soul price graph over your portfolio, so you can read the market without leaving the menu. Oil prices are also what the fuel pump charges you, and what a letter to another dimension costs.

real_estate.title: Real Estate
real_estate.description: There are thirty properties spread across every town, rated from one to five stars. One to three star properties are cheap dumps, and a one star place costs under a thousand euros. Four and five star places are estates. Two ways to hold one: - BUY it outright. You own it, and you can offer it for rent to NPCs for income, collected at midnight and on the first of the month. - RENT it as a tenant. A recurring monthly cost, you cannot sublet, and missing payments evicts you and puts the property back on the market. Prices move with procedural NEWS events tied to specific towns, so a headline about a town is a signal about its property. Renting a ROOM is a different thing entirely: an inn room is booked for 24 game hours, and the booking is written into the world, so no other savegame of that world can take that same bed on the same day. They will be told who has it.

owning_a_shop.title: Owning a Shop
owning_a_shop.description: You can own shops, and running one is a real business rather than a passive income trickle. A shop holds stock, a warehouse and a production line. Items with recipes can be PRODUCED from materials on the premises, deliveries are made at delivery points on the maps, and NPC staff can be hired to do the work. The management screen has four pages: an overview, the stock on the shelves, the warehouse behind them, and the catalogue of what could be produced. Choosing a slot on the stock page takes you to the catalogue to pick what that slot makes.

work.title: Work
work.description: Beyond quests there is honest labour: more than thirty jobs across several categories, any of which any party member can be sent to do. Each job states its stat requirements before you start. You are warned if the chosen member is short of them, but never stopped: risky work is allowed and sometimes pays. A shift takes real game time, the screen darkens for it, and the outcome is generated from the worker's stats and their luck. You earn money, and you can also LOSE it in a disaster, take damage, or come out with a status effect from an accident. The Job Offers menu lists what is available right now and where, with duration and hourly pay, so you can pick the shift that is worth the walk.

quests.title: Quests
quests.description: Quests are generated rather than authored, in the manner of Daggerfall, and a quest board is all the setup one needs: the offers on it are derived from where the board stands. Every quest is a list of STEPS. A simple one has a single step; a chain has two or three, done in order or in any order. The steps are real detection primitives wired into the rest of the game, which is why quests can ask for almost anything: - get to a set of world coordinates, or to a named destination - open an auto placed chest, or dig a site (which needs a shovel) - land on a planet and open its sample cache - kill a specific high level enemy, force spawned at a tile, which stays there until it is killed even if the quest fails - scan statues or signposts at a site - actually dismantle a number of trees, rocks or piles of rubble - open the quest board of another town - interview a citizen of a destination through the Empathize panel - hand over items at claim time - wait for goods to arrive - win arena fights, defeat a number of enemies, or hold a number of oil shares Every contract's terms are generated with the offer and disclosed BEFORE you accept: the reward, the upfront cost, the advance paid to you, the deadline, the penalty for failing, the bounty for breaching it, and the reputation it moves. Scams lie. That is the point of them. Rewards and difficulty scale on the party's median level. The board's second tab lists your signed contracts with their progress and countdowns, and lets you collect or abandon, which triggers the failure clauses and says so. The quest log itself is a kanban board of sticky notes in three columns, to do, in progress and done, which you can drag between columns.

reading_a_notice.title: Reading a Notice
reading_a_notice.description: A quest notice is written in the VOICE of whoever pinned it up. There are dozens of faction registers and a couple of dozen personality registers, and they read completely differently: a corporate contract, a goblin scrawl, a redacted military bill, a nervous private plea. That voice is information. What is left out, what is over explained and what is obviously a lie are all readable before you accept, and the terms panel tells you the rest.

arcade_tokens.title: Arcade Tokens
arcade_tokens.description: Arcade machines take tokens, not money. Tokens are bought with euros at the converter machine, or from the Token Exchange application on the Hypernet, and unused tokens can be cashed back in. Both quote the same rate, so there is no arbitrage to find. There is, however, a gold converter for the impatient.

the_workbench.title: The Workbench
the_workbench.description: The Thinker is the general workbench: assembling things and taking them apart. A recipe is written on the item itself, so the item is the authority. Assembling consumes the materials listed; disassembling salvages an item back into pieces. The workbench hides a recipe until it has been made once, which makes it the opposite of the forge: it rewards experiment, and the encyclopedia fills as you work. Some things everybody already knows how to make, and those are on the board from the start. Base crafting materials are a fixed set that everything else is built from, and they come from dismantling the world: felling trees, mining rocks, breaking furniture, salvaging gear.

the_forge.title: The Forge
the_forge.description: The forge is the workbench with the opposite philosophy: it hides NOTHING. Every weapon and armour in the game is on the board from your first visit, and what changes as you train is which of them your hands can actually make. Four tabs: what you can smith right now, what you could make but lack the materials for (with how many lines of the bill are short), what is too complex for your training (with the tier it is waiting for), and what this party has already forged. Around thirty one TRADES are in play, one per item, so the board is not all hammers: a robe is Tailoring, a wig is Wig Making, a costume is Cosplay, a ring is Jewelry Making, a rifle is Gunsmithing, a circuit woven coat is Electronics. NOTHING LEAVES THE ANVIL AS A COPY. Each finished piece is registered as its own entry with its own identity, which is why two of them never stack, and it carries a sheet nobody else's copy has. Three things decide that sheet: how far past the required tier the smith's trade is trained, how rich the bill that went into the crucible was, and the heat on the day. Every parameter then drifts on its own, and the price follows, so a masterwork climbs the rarity ladder by itself. Finishes are offered as a strip of swatches, and the preview is a promise: the seed the 3D model is turned under is rolled once, shown to you, and then kept on the piece. The SMELT button melts a carried piece back down into its materials: half the bill, and more from a piece that was well made. Whoever is at the anvil is everything. The party switcher decides which tab an entry falls into, whether the forge button lights, and who earns the specialization points for the work.

alchemistry.title: Alchemistry
alchemistry.description: Every alchemical recipe is unlocked and readable from the start. Nothing is gated behind a class. A recipe is COPIED onto one of the benches, and it is the bench you edit and run, so the same recipe can be set up two different ways at once. WHETHER IT WORKS IS A SKILL CHECK. Each recipe demands a set of specializations at a minimum tier. Meeting every requirement puts the failure chance at exactly zero. Each tier short of any requirement adds to the failure chance, so a short handed alchemist can still try, and will often ruin the batch. Tiers held ABOVE what a recipe asks are not wasted: they pay out as extra product, one more flask per couple of surplus tiers, up to a cap. TIME IS THE WORLD CLOCK. A step's duration is game minutes, so a batch keeps cooking while you walk, work a shift, travel or sleep, and finishes the moment the clock says it should. A bench set to REPEAT rebuys its reagents and starts again the instant it finishes, and stands down with a warning when the pack can no longer pay for a run.

cooking.title: Cooking
cooking.description: Cooking combines two recovery items into one better one. The first item's recovery is doubled and the second's is added on top, so the ORDER matters. Cooking two of the same thing produces an adjective instead: a random one, which carries a bonus or a penalty to the effect. The name of the result is built from the two ingredients, first word of the first and last word of the second. Because food carries calories, fat and protein, cooking is also nutrition management: a cooked meal is worth what went into it.

brewing.title: Brewing
brewing.description: Barrels ferment. You load a barrel, leave it, and time does the work: brewing and distilling run on the world clock like everything else, and the barrels standing on the maps belong to the world rather than to your savegame. It is the slowest crafting in the game and the least demanding of your attention, which is rather the point.

building_and_furniture.title: Building and Furniture
building_and_furniture.description: The Build menu places furniture on tiles, snapped to the grid. Pieces can be crafted from materials, bought, and dismantled again to recover materials. Multi tile pieces are supported, and some pieces can be flipped. There are rules about where things go: wall furniture only goes on walls, the upper tiles of ordinary furniture may overlap a wall but the lower tiles may not, and some terrain refuses furniture altogether. What you have built belongs to the WORLD, per coordinate, so a room you furnished is furnished for every savegame of that world. What is still in your pack, and which recipes you have unlocked, stay yours. The Build menu is also where ANIMALS are bought: pick one and click a tile to place it.

farming.title: Farming
farming.description: Any tilled soil can be farmed, and plants have a real lifecycle driven by the clock, the season and the weather. - Plants only grow during their own seasons. Out of season they are dormant and no time accumulates. - Rain speeds growth by 30%, a storm by 10%, and snow slows it by half. - A greenhouse map runs at full speed all year and multiplies growth further. - A plant at 100% is harvested on the spot when you interact with it; the management menu only opens on a plot still growing. On the procedural map, tilled soil is farmable too. The first visit to a world square rolls, from the world seed, which contiguous patches are already sown and with what, so a whole field grows the same crop. Those plots live in the world folder, so a field sown, grown or harvested in one savegame is the same field in every other savegame of that world.

animals.title: Animals
animals.description: Animals are bought in the Build menu and placed on a tile. They are managed from the Assets screen, where each is a livestock asset you can collect from, sell, or turn into a pet. They GROW: from baby to adult over a set number of days on the world clock, and adults produce at intervals. What they pay out is what a living animal gives, an egg, a pail of milk, a fleece, never what you would get by killing it. Every animal also carries a COMPANY value, paid into the party's social need whenever you interact with it: the leader in full, everyone else at half, once per game day per animal so it cannot be farmed. A dog, a donkey and a rooster produce nothing at all and are kept for exactly this reason. An animal is remembered against the world coordinate it was placed at, so it is still there when you come back.

beekeeping.title: Beekeeping
beekeeping.description: A hive is a full colony simulation, not a container that fills up. There are castes: a queen, workers, nurses, guards, foragers and drones, each with a lifecycle from egg through larva and pupa to adult and death. The comb is drawn as hexagons and the colony produces honey, pollen, royal jelly and wax. Seasons and weather act on it, disease and pests threaten it, and the colony has moods and efficiency that answer to how it is kept. The apiary belongs to the world, so it keeps living between savegames.

procedural_artifacts.title: Procedural Artifacts
procedural_artifacts.description: Artifacts are generated items, weapons and armour with rolled properties. They turn up in loot, in vaults, at the end of adventures, and out of certain rites. They belong to the world, which is why an artifact left behind by one party is the same artifact another finds. There is also a rite that turns a PARTY MEMBER into a weapon. It is exactly what it sounds like.

how_loot_is_rolled.title: How Loot Is Rolled
how_loot_is_rolled.description: Random loot is scored from 0 to 100 by adding the party's MEDIAN level to a difficulty modifier the place itself carries. A low modifier makes a gentle area, a high one makes a dangerous area generous. That score picks the rarity band: - around 0 to 20, almost everything is common - 25 to 45, a mix of common and uncommon - 50, a balanced spread - 75, more epic and legendary - 100, almost everything is legendary Rarity is read off price, and the same ladder colours item names everywhere: the backpack, the shop, the reward popup, the container list. A patron's vault is the one place where the tables are pushed hard toward the expensive end on purpose.

containers.title: Containers
containers.description: Containers hold things, without limit, and each one is unique to its map and event. Their contents are generated from the categories they declare, weighted by rarity, and once generated they belong to the world. The EXTRADIMENSIONAL container is the exception and the most useful item in the game: it can be opened from anywhere, and it is the party's own, not the world's. So are the holds of the camper and the car. Between them, those three are the answer to carrying capacity.

the_star_map.title: The Star Map
the_star_map.description: The star map is a real time 3D view of the universe, drawn at several SCALES: the system you are in, the galaxy around it, the local group, the supercluster, the filaments of the cosmic web, and the observable universe itself. At system scale one unit is one astronomical unit, and bodies are drawn larger than life so they can be seen at all: true scale would make every planet invisible. Drag to orbit, wheel to zoom, arrows or the stick to nudge what you are looking at. Clicking a body selects it, and the panel that opens says what it is and offers what you can do with it: travel there, or land. Everything is lit properly. Planets have day and night terminators that track their actual star, cloud layers that turn independently, atmospheres, rings, and star surfaces that boil.

travelling_between_stars.title: Travelling Between Stars
travelling_between_stars.description: Select a system and travel to it. The journey takes time and burns FUEL, and the ship's fuel is the thing that decides how far you can go. REFUELLING has one rule worth knowing: only an ordinary fusing star can power a refuel. Main sequence stars of every class will do it; remnants, brown dwarfs and black holes will not. The Refuel command works this out for you: - parked at a fusing star already, it just starts the pumps - with a fusing star elsewhere in this system, it plots the short hop - otherwise it plots a course to the nearest system that has one Either way the pumps engage by themselves the moment you arrive. While you are aboard the ship, the view through the windows is the real one: on any map inside the ship the background shows where you actually are, the planet you are orbiting or the star you are parked at, and it streaks and scrolls while you are under way.

your_starship.title: Your Starship
your_starship.description: The ship is generated, not drawn. Hull, layout, plating, panel lines, livery, decals, lit windows and wear are all built procedurally, and the DEFAULT appearance is derived from your world's seed, so a given world always starts with the same ship. From the vehicle menu you can change its appearance: reroll the whole thing, or step through individual traits one at a time and keep the rest. What you choose is stored, and everything you do not choose stays derived from the seed. The ship is where the crew lives. Under way, they tend one need at a time, a meal, a wash, a conversation, a game, a shift of sleep, changing their minds halfway through as often as not. Eating consumes real food out of the hold, and with an empty hold they go and do something else instead.

landing.title: Landing
landing.description: Orbiting a planet, you can land. Where there are landing sites you are offered the list of them; otherwise you touch down on the surface. An alien surface is a real explorable map, generated the same way Earth's are but from a different palette entirely: there are dozens of ALIEN BIOMES, chosen by the type of world you landed on, so an ice giant's moon is nothing like a carbon planet. The rules out there are not Earth's rules: - Encounters are not scaled to your party or to your distance from home. The WORLD's own level decides, rolled per planet, and you can read it off the planet's biosignature before you commit. - There is nothing to forage. Another world's flora is not a hedgerow. What it offers is butchered off the local wildlife instead. - What has been dug out of each body is remembered in the world folder, so a body you have stripped stays stripped for every savegame of that world. Everything you find out there is written into the diary, and species you identify go into the bestiary's alien page.

anomalies.title: Anomalies
anomalies.description: Every star system that holds planets carries at least one anomalous world, marked with a question mark on the map. Holding orbit over it offers to INVESTIGATE, once and only once. What follows is a branching encounter written for that kind of world: every choice leads somewhere and the last node pays out, in a relic, in salvage, in a fight with something native, or in the walk back with nothing. It is the same engine as the adventures on Earth's own map, so the same things are true of it: the prose is combinatorial and never reads the same way twice, your companion comments on it in their own voice, and some choices are only offered to a leader of the right temperament.

what_is_out_there.title: What Is Out There
what_is_out_there.description: The universe is not a field of identical dots. STARS come in the real classes and in a couple of dozen exotic kinds besides, each with its own model: remnants, brown dwarfs, feeding X-ray binaries, and stranger things. Systems can be binary or have several stars, and you travel to each star of a system individually. BLACK HOLES come in three weights, and the largest are drawn as lensed billboards in the manner of Interstellar, with an accretion stream that coils and takes the whole separation as its length. ROGUE PLANETS drift between the stars with no sun at all. NEBULAE include about twenty real ones, placed at their real galactic coordinates and hand shaped: the Horsehead, the Orion Nebula, the dark nebulae and others. DYSON SPHERES exist, and so do things nobody has explained. Above the galaxy the map keeps going: the local group, superclusters, the filaments of the cosmic web, and the shells of the observable universe. Our own solar system is in there, hand authored, with its twelve real bodies, its belts and a working shell of orbital debris.

patron_worlds.title: Patron Worlds
patron_worlds.description: Some worlds in other galaxies are named after the people who paid for the game. They are habitable and life bearing, they orbit exotic objects, they sit in nine planet systems where no two planets share a type, and they are listed in the star map catalogue under Patrons. Each of those people also owns a HATCH somewhere on the world map, on exactly one square, which cannot be dismantled and which nothing ever grows over. Going down it opens their vault: a great hall with strongrooms and a deep back chamber, dressed almost entirely in gold and weapons, with every chest the template can hold. While you are down there the loot tables are weighted hard toward the expensive end. Where those hatches are is encrypted in the game's own data, keyed on the coordinates themselves, so nothing is spoiled by reading the file. Finding one is finding one.

the_night_sky.title: The Night Sky
the_night_sky.description: Separate from the star map there is a night sky chart: a draggable, zoomable planisphere with stars sized by magnitude, constellations traced in gold, a decorative right ascension and declination grid, and a soft Milky Way band. Tab switches between constellation sets, European and Chinese, which trace completely different figures across the same stars. Confirm recenters and fits the whole sky on the screen.

the_hypernet_desktop.title: The Hypernet Desktop
the_hypernet_desktop.description: The Hypernet is a whole simulated operating system, drawn in the style of the period: a desktop, a taskbar, a start menu, windows you drag and resize, and a set of applications that are all real programs rather than menu screens. It has its own virtual FILE SYSTEM and registry, and both are saved inside your savegame, so files you write and settings you change persist. Controls: - WASD or the arrow keys move the focus ring between interactive elements. - Tab and Shift Tab cycle through them. - Enter or Space activates whatever is focused. - Escape leaves a text field, then closes the active window, then exits. - The controller d-pad navigates, A activates, B closes the window or exits, and the left stick is a free mouse cursor. Everything below is an application on that desktop.
